What does Owen say is the error of New Testament believers who try to pray by relying on the same gifts and aids used under the Old Testament?

Owen argues that New Testament believers who "pretence of what was done under the Old, is to reject the grace of the gospel, and to make themselves guilty of the highest ingratitude" are committing a serious fault. He warns that such people are refusing the promised Spirit of grace that God has pledged By clinging to former practices, they "annihilate the promise" and betray the gratitude owed to the gospel’s grace.

meta.heading: [Owen — Works Vol04]
meta.passage:
For persons under the New Testament, who are com- 
manded to pray, not to make use constantly in their so doing of the 
gifts, aids, and assistances of the Spirit, which are peculiarly dispensed 
and communicated therein, on pretence of what was done under the 
Old, is to reject the grace of the gospel, and to make themselves 
guilty of the highest ingratitude. Wherefore, although we may and 
ought to bear with them who, having not received any thing of this 
promised grace and assistance, nor believing there is any such thing, 
do plead for the use of forms of prayer to be composed by some and 
read by others or themselves, and that only, in the discharge of this 
duty; yet such as have been made partakers of this grace, and who 
owm it their duty constantly to use and improve the promised aids 
of the Spirit of God, will be careful not to admit of any such prin- 
ciples or practice as would plainly annihilate the promise. 

Thus much, then, we may suppose ourselves to have obtained in 
the consideration of this testimony. That God hath promised under 
the New Testament to give unto believers, in a plentiful manner or 
measure, the Spirit of grace and of supplications, or his own Holy 
Spirit, enabling them to piray according to his mind and will. 
The way and manner of his work therein shall be afterward declared. 
And it may suffice to oppose, in general, this one promise unto the 
open reproaches and bold contempts that are by many cast on the 
Spirit of prayer; whose framers, unless they can blot this text out of 
the Scripture, will fail at last in their design.

According to Brooks, what is the first remedy he proposes for dealing with the multitude of vain thoughts Satan casts into the soul?

Brooks teaches that the initial remedy is to pray that one's heart be strongly affected by the greatness, holiness, majesty, and glory of God. He writes, "Pray that your hearts may be strongly affected with the greatness, holiness, majesty, and glory, of that God before whom you stand, and with whom your souls converse in religious services." This prayerful focus on God's omniscience, omnipresence, and omnipotence is presented as the primary means to keep vain thoughts at bay.

According to Manton, how does a true Christian’s reliance on God differ from merely using Him as a refuge?

Manton teaches that a true Christian must not treat God merely as a temporary shelter for moments of crisis but should make Him the permanent dwelling of his soul. He explains that "a refuge is the place of our retreat in a time of danger ; an habitation is the place of our residence in a time of peace," and warns that most people "run to it in a storm, but do not fix their residence there." Rather than seeking God only when "all other means and refuges fail them," the believer is to "dwell in God, not run to him now and then," echoing the psalmist’s declaration that "He that dwelleth in the secret place of the Most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty." This constant communion distinguishes genuine habitation from occasional refuge.

Why does Edwards say that the disposition to approve the beauty of justice’s uniformity and proportion is not true virtue?

Edwards teaches that while the uniformity and proportion of justice "the tendency of general benevolence to produce justice" can please a virtuous mind because it tends toward the general good, the mere disposition to approve this kind of beauty is not itself a virtue. He argues that this approval is "entirely a different thing from a truly virtuous taste" and therefore lacks the nature of true virtue.

According to Spurgeon in this sermon, how does a church member’s inconsistency affect the whole congregation?

Spurgeon teaches that a single member’s inconsistency can jeopardize the reputation of the entire church. He warns that "any member whom we receive into this Church may compromise all the rest" and that when a member is found in To whom do you belong?\"That man sinned not alone." Thus each believer must guard his own conduct, lest he imperil the honor of the whole body of Christ.

meta.heading: [Sermon 3079 — "A Searching Question"]
meta.passage:
You can generally read a man's character in his boy's face and in his boy's conduct and conversation. We should remember this and see that we send our children forth not needing to be ashamed that they should tell to whom they belong! The same is the case with regard to Church members. Any member whom we receive into this Church may compromise all the rest. If any one member is found in bad or suspicious company, the question is sure to be asked, "To whom do you belong?" Instead of laying down his delinquencies at his own door as being inconsistent, men are quite sure to put them at our door. The minister is generally the horse that is saddled with his people's sins. He would willingly bear them on his own heart in deep humiliation before God if he knew that his people also would bear them in penitence before God. Let every Church member remember that he imperils the honor of the whole Church by his inconsistency--and it may be said of him, "That man sinned not alone."

This, however, is not my main point tonight. I am going to aim at something which directly affects our eternal position and standing before God. I shall first open up the question in a different sense from that in which it was asked by David. Then, secondly, I will try to guide you in your response. And when I have done that, I will give a few words of good advice to those who have individually and respectively to furnish the answer.

First, then, "TO WHOM DO YOU BELONG?"

This is a question of universal pertinence.

According to Manton in Works Vol10, why is Jesus Christ identified as the sole judge of the world?

Manton teaches that the ultimate authority to judge rests in Christ because God Himself is the wronged party offended by human sin. He writes, "He is the wronged party, and offended with the sins of men," and explains that God's essential glory is immutable and cannot be lessened or increased by any human action. Since the divine glory remains unchanged regardless of obedience or disobedience, only the supreme power appointed by God—Jesus Christ—can render judgment and make amends for the wrongs done to both body and reputation.

meta.passage:
I shall the longer insist on this, because the 
main hinge of all lieth here, and this doth bring the matter home. 
That Jesus Christ, and none but Jesus Christ, shall be the world's 
judge. By the law of nature, the wronged party and the supreme 
power hath right to require satisfaction for the wrong done. Where 
no power is publicly constituted, possibly the wronged party hath

matter, and to make amends to those that are wronged in their body,

According to the sermon, what is one of the first noticeable changes in a person when the Grace of God begins its work in his soul?

Spurgeon teaches that the initial effect of the Grace of God on a new believer is a shift toward seriousness and thoughtfulness. He writes that "When a man becomes a Christian and the Grace of God commences its work in his soul, he learns to be serious and thoughtful." This new seriousness leads the believer to renounce former carelessness, become sober and considerate, and develop a deep concern for his own character before God, especially regarding the temptations he may encounter.

meta.heading: [Sermon 1506 — "Choice Comfort for a Young Believer"]
meta.passage:
Now, between half-past twelve o'clock this morning and this time in the evening such souls have gone a day's journey towards Heaven and already they have begun, I dare say, to question themselves and possibly to be exercised with some few fears. Thus early they may have met with lions in the way, or have found worse than real lions in their own fears. They have only lately known the Lord, but already they are growing anxious and looking into the future with a somewhat troubled gaze. Therefore we come forth lovingly as a shepherd hastens to cherish the newborn lambs. We come to the little ones with words of good cheer, for they need them and we have special orders from our Master to see that they are tenderly comforted.

We trust to also speak to those who have known the Lord for many years, some words of help with regard to matters which may now be causing them alarm. The consolations of the Lord are very reviving and they abound in number, therefore let small and great partake of them. "Comfort you, comfort you My people, says your God." When a man becomes a Christian and the Grace of God commences its work in his soul, he learns to be serious and thoughtful. That is one of the first noticeable changes in him. He renounces his former carelessness and indifference and becomes a sober, considerate man in whose mind there is a deep concern as to his own character in the sight of God. He is concerned about the temptations he meets with in his walk among the sons of men lest these temptations should be too much for him and he should be betrayed into sin.

According to Bayly’s ‘Practice Of Piety’, what are the six specific purposes for observing a baptism with reverent attention?

Bayly teaches that when baptism is to be administered the observer should stay and behold it with reverent attention for six distinct purposes. First, the believer must “First, Shew thy reverence to God's ordinance;” thereby honoring the divine command. Second, one should consider “the better consider thine own ingrafting into the visible body of Christ's church,” reflecting on personal incorporation into the body of Christ. Third, the observer is to “repay thy debts, in praying for the infant which is to be baptized,” interceding that God grants the infant the inward effects of baptism. Fourth, the faithful should “assist the church in praising God for grafting another member into his mystical body,” joining the corporate worship. Fifth, the believer is to “prove whether the effects of Christ's death killeth sin in thee, and whether thou be raised to newness of life by the virtue of his resurrection,” examining the transformative power of the gospel. Sixth, one must affirming a participatory role in the church. These six purposes together shape a reverent and reflective posture toward baptism.

What does Manton say ministers should prioritize in their preaching?

Manton teaches that ministers must focus on for the present age, rather than wasting effort on obsolete controversies. He warns that "It is but a cheap zeal that declaimeth against antiquated errors, and things now out of use and practice," and that preaching old errors is like Therefore, the proper aim is to deliver seasonable, needed truths that the people can bear.

What does Increase Mather report happened to the godly man named Partridge in July 1654?

Increase Mather records that in July 1654 a man named Partridge, described as "a Man whose Name was Partridge (esteemed a very godly person)", was struck down by a storm. How does the sermon explain the way believers receive the divine nature without becoming gods?

Spurgeon teaches that believers are "made partakers of the Divine Nature" in the sense of receiving the same character and becoming children of God, rather than receiving the essence of Deity itself. He explains that the fullness of the Godhead dwells in Christ, and through Him the divine grace is communicated to those who come by faith, so that they receive rather than contribute to salvation. This reception allows them to later dispense "rivers of living water" to others.

meta.heading: [Sermon 1169 — "The Fullness of Christ the Treasury of the Saints"]
meta.passage:
But this golden Vessel, though heated, was not melted! It could contain the Divine fire and yet not be destroyed--and now in Christ Jesus dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily and, moreover, the Divine Nature is in Him in such a way as to be capable of communication to the sons of men. Of course the essence of Deity is not communicated, for that would be to make men into Gods--but we are "made partakers of the Divine Nature" in the sense of receiving the same character--and becoming the children of God. That which God could not bring to us directly by reason of our inability to receive it, He has now brought to us through a Mediator, by placing it in the Man, Christ Jesus, that we, coming to Him, might freely receive of it.

The next step in the plan of salvation is this--that after the fullness of God has come to man in the Person of His Son, everyone that comes to Him by faith receives His Divine Grace. Salvation is not by what you bring to Christ, but by what you take from Him. You are to be receivers first, and then, by-and-by, through the power of Grace, you shall give forth from yourselves rivers of living water to others. In your first coming you come empty, having nothing but your sin and misery--as empty, undeserving sinners you receive of His fullness--and all your life continue to do the same.

How does Edwards differentiate between God's perceptive will and His disposing will when explaining the sincerity of divine commands, counsels, and invitations?

Edwards argues that the sincerity of God's commands, counsels, and invitations is grounded in what he calls God's perceptive will, not in a deterministic disposing will. He explains that even if events are ordained as necessary, God can still “sincerely command and require” man to act, because such commands flow from the perceptive will that reflects what God loves and what is agreeable to the human heart. As he puts it, "Counsels and invitations are manifestations of God's perceptive will, or of what God loves, and what is in itself, and as man's act, agreeable to his heart ; and not of his disposing will, and what he chooses as a part of his own infinite scheme of things." Thus, divine commands remain sincere and genuine, despite any underlying necessity.

Why does the sermon say the Lord chose Abram from Ur of the Chaldees?

Spurgeon teaches that the Lord’s selection of Abram from Ur of the Chaldees is an act of divine sovereignty, for which Scripture gives no explicit reason. He notes that Abram’s family, as the passage quotes Joshua, "Your fathers dwelt on the other side of the flood in old time, even Terah, the father of Abraham and the father of Nachor--and they served other gods," yet the Lord still called Abram alone and blessed him, demonstrating His sovereign choice beyond human understanding.

meta.heading: [Sermon 2011 — "Abram's Call--or, Half-Way--and All the Way"]
meta.passage:
And therefore before the lamp of God had wholly gone out, the Lord determined to reveal Himself and establish His worship in the world. He would select a family to be His peculiar servants. He would manifest Himself to the father of that family and would make with him a Covenant. He would reveal to him the great things which He intended to do in the fullness of time and He would bid him hand down the Revelation to his children from generation to generation.

This family should grow into a nation and to that nation should be committed the oracles of God. Out of that nation should come Prophets and priests and heroes who should believe in God and maintain the true faith against all comers, even until the Son of God Himself should come to manifest the glory of God in a preeminent degree. In the midst of that nation the Lord resolved to set up ordinances and a settled organization by which Truth should be taught through type and symbol and by the hallowed speech of godly men. This, in His wisdom, He judged to be best for the future of the race.

In the wise sovereignty of His choice, the Lord chose Abram and his house. He gives no account of his matters and we cannot, therefore, tell why he took out of Ur of the Chaldees those of whom Joshua says, "Your fathers dwelt on the other side of the flood in old time, even Terah, the father of Abraham and the father of Nachor--and they served other gods." The Lord called Abram alone and blessed him.

How does Calvin distinguish between natural human wisdom and the "wisdom of this world" mentioned by Paul?

Calvin explains that natural perspicacity, the liberal arts, and all sciences are inherently "gifts of God." However, he clarifies that these gifts are confined within their own limits and "cannot penetrate" into God's heavenly kingdom. Their proper function is to serve as a handmaid, not a mistress, and they must be "entirely subject to the word and Spirit of God." The "wisdom of the world," in Paul's acceptation, refers to these gifts when they assume authority for themselves, refusing to be regulated by God's word or to yield in complete subjection to Him. If they set themselves in opposition to Christ, they are to be regarded as dangerous pests and hindrances. Therefore, an individual is considered wise in the world's account but foolish in God's estimation until they acknowledge that all true knowledge comes from God and resign themselves unreservedly to Christ's guidance.

How does Howe illustrate the soul's capacity to act independently of corporeal organs?

Howe illustrates the soul's capacity to act independently of corporeal organs by explaining that the soul's very use of these organs implies an action antecedent to their assistance. He posits that the soul "supposes an operation upon them, antecedent to any operation by them." As an example, he notes that when one uses a pen, one first acts upon it to impress motion, an action that does not itself require another instrument. This suggests that the soul's action upon an organ must ultimately occur without the ministry of any organ, to avoid an infinite regress of bodies. Furthermore, Howe argues that even when separated from the body, the soul is not diminished but can still He compares the soul's inability to perform "meaner, and grosser pieces of drudgerie" out of the body to a magistrate not personally executing a malefactor, emphasizing that this does not signify disparagement or diminution of its proper functions.

What contrast does Spurgeon draw between the childhood understanding of God's role in nature and the views of the 'proudly enlightened age'?

Spurgeon highlights a stark contrast between the simple, truthful understanding of God's active involvement in creation, as taught in childhood, and the complex, God-excluding theories prevalent in a 'proudly enlightened age.' He recounts how mothers taught children, through hymns like Watts', that "My God, who makes the sun to know His proper hour to rise, And to give light to all below, Does send him round the skies." This truth, he argues, is being challenged by modern "schools of philosophy and science" that are "spinning all sorts of theories to get rid of God, to turn our Benefactor out of His own world and put man's best Friend as far away as possible." Spurgeon suggests that these skeptical teachers would benefit from returning to a simpler faith, recognizing that and that "Laws of Nature can do nothing without a power at the back of the laws."

meta.heading: [Sermon 1414 — "No Difference"]
meta.passage:
Watts taught us to sing when we were children--

"My God, who makes the sun to know

His proper hour to rise,

And to give light to all below,

Does send him round the skies." So our mothers taught us and they taught us the truth. But the very wise men of this proudly enlightened age seem to be spinning all sorts of theories to get rid of God, to turn our Benefactor out of His own world and put man's best Friend as far away as possible.

I am sometimes reminded by these schools of philosophy and science of Tom Hood's, "I remember, I remember." Here is a verse of it--

"I remember, I remember, The fir trees dark and high I used to think their slender tops Were close against the sky. It was a childish ignorance, But now 'tis little joy To know I'm farther off from Hea ven Than when I was a boy."

It were a good thing for our skeptical teachers who have banished God out of His own universe if they could go back to their mothers' knees and learn to talk simply and naturally after the fashion of the wisest man that ever lived, namely, our Lord and Master. Then would they also confess that our heavenly Father "makes His sun to rise and He sends the rain," for so it is. Laws of Nature can do nothing without a power at the back of the laws. What is Nature, about which many infidels speak so very plentifully? Ask them to tell you what Nature is and they will reply, "Why, it is Nature." Well, but what is that?

What does Manton teach about the proper response when experiencing God's 'mighty hand' or heavy affliction?

Manton teaches that when under God's 'mighty hand' or experiencing heavy affliction, believers should acknowledge God's justice and avoid questioning His providences. He states that "The Lord takes it ill when you question any of his providences." Instead of reproaching God when His hand is 'smart and heavy upon you,' one should remember that "affliction opens the eyes of the worst men." Manton cites Nebuchadnezzar as an example, who, after being chastised, came to praise God, declaring, "Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and extol and honour the king of heaven, all whose works are truth, and his ways judgment, and those that walk in pride he is able to abase." This response involves recognizing that God governs all things righteously and will be clear and justified in all His judgments and actions for the punishment of sin.

Does the Westminster Confession teach that unlearned individuals can understand the necessary truths for salvation from Scripture?

The Westminster Confession affirms that while not all parts of Scripture are equally clear, the essential truths for salvation are presented plainly enough for all. It teaches that "those things which are necessary to be known, believed, and observed, for salvation, are so clearly propounded and opened in some place of scripture or other, that not only the learned, but the unlearned, in a due use of the ordinary means, may attain unto a sufficient understanding of them." This means that diligent engagement with the Bible, using ordinary means, allows even those without extensive education to comprehend what is required for salvation.

What characteristics define the "fine picture of a man perfect and upright before God" as exemplified by Job in his self-defense?

Spurgeon teaches that Job's self-defense, despite some human frailties, presents "a fine picture of a man perfect and upright before God." This ideal is characterized by a deep consciousness of perfect integrity and an unwavering commitment to God's ways, even when facing false accusations and severe distress. A person embodying this ideal is able to declare truthfully, as Job did, "My foot has held His steps, His way have I kept and not declined. Neither have I gone back from the commandment of His lips; I have esteemed the words of His mouth more than my necessary food." This demonstrates a life where God's commandments are treasured above all else, serving as a "high ideal after which every Christian should strive."

meta.heading: [Sermon 1526 — "The Fair Portrait of a Saint"]
meta.passage:
Let them stand as a warning to us never to judge men by their circumstances and never to conclude that a man must be wicked because he has fallen from riches to poverty.

Job, however, knew his innocence and he was determined not to give way to them. He said, "You are forgers of lies, physicians of no value. O that you would altogether hold your peace and it should be your wisdom!" He fought the battle right manfully. Not, perhaps, without a little display of temper and self-righteousness, but still, with much less of either than any of us would have shown had we been in the same plight and had we been equally conscious of perfect integrity. He has, in this part of his self-defense, sketched a fine picture of a man perfect and upright before God. He has set before us the image to which we should seek to be conformed. Here is the high ideal after which every Christian should strive and happy shall he be who shall attain to it.

Blessed is he who, in the hour of his distress, if he is falsely accused, will be able to say with as much truth as the Patriarch could, "My foot has held His steps, His way have I kept and not declined. Neither have I gone back from the commandment of His lips; I have esteemed the words of His mouth more than my necessary food." I ask you, first, to inspect the picture of Job's holy life, that you may make it your model. After we have done this, we will look a little below the surface, asking the question, "How was he enabled to lead such an admirable life as this.

What does Spurgeon teach about the meaning of suffering and adversity in a believer's life?

Spurgeon teaches that present suffering, such as poverty, desertion, and disease, does not indicate God's anger or judgment against a righteous individual. He emphasizes that "neither disease, nor bereavements, nor poverty, can prove a man to be wicked, nor do they even hint that the chosen are divided from the hearts of Christ." Instead, he encourages believers to "settle it in your hearts that men are not to be judged according to their present circumstances," and to understand their ultimate end, like David, which helps prevent them from "writing bitter things against yourselves in the time of trouble."

meta.heading: [Sermon 410 — "Not Now, But Hereafter!"]
meta.passage:
In my very soul I feel that if evil days shall come upon me, if poverty, desertion, and disease should place me upon Job's dunghill, I shall point to that sermon with pleasure, and say to those who will tell me that God is angry with me, and has judged me to be unworthy, "Nay, ye know not what ye say, for the judgment is not passed already, nor is this the field of execution; neither disease, nor bereavements, nor poverty, can prove a man to be wicked, nor do they even hint that the chosen are divided from the hearts of Christ." O my beloved friends, settle it in your hearts that men are not to be judged according to their present circumstances, and learn like David to understand their end. It will save you from writing bitter things against yourselves in the time of trouble, and prevent your scanning the works of Providence, and measuring the infinite by line and plummet.

It is mainly my business, today, to deal with those who may wickedly continue in sin because their judgment tarries. If the Lord does not in this world visit the ungodly with stripes, this is but the surer evidence that in the world to come there is a solemn retribution for the impenitent. If the affliction which is here accorded to men be not the punishment of sin, we turn to Scripture and discover what that punishment will be, and we are soon informed that it is something far heavier than any calamities which occur in this life,--something infinitely more tremendous than the most disastrous accident, the most shocking mutilation, or the most painful death.

According to this sermon, what characterizes the state of a Christian who has lost the brightness of his evidences?

Spurgeon describes a Christian who has lost the brightness of his evidences as one who looks on the past with pleasure, the future with dread, and the present with sorrow. This individual fondly remembers past days in the fear of the Lord as "being the sweetest and the best they have ever had," wishing for their young days over again to live near to Jesus. However, their present is "clad in a sable garb of gloom and dreariness," marked by a feeling of having wandered from Christ or that he has hidden his face. While they once had no doubt of their salvation and could confidently declare, "I know whom I have believed," they now experience "all cloud" where there was once none, and are troubled by the dark thought that they "was a hypocrite, and had deceived myself and others."

Brooks teaches that the eternal Godhead of Christ is a "point of high concernment" because it is "the rock of our salvation," and anyone who does not build upon this truth "buildeth upon the sands." According to Hodge’s commentary, how does Paul illustrate the relationship between Adam and Christ in Romans 5?

Hodge explains that Paul first establishes the typology by showing that Adam "was really the representative of his race," meaning that all humanity shares in Adam’s offense and its consequent death. After making this point, Paul declares Adam "a type of Christ," and then proceeds to qualify the comparison by detailing the specific aspects of the analogy in verses 15‑17. This method highlights the contrast between the sin of Adam and the righteousness of Christ.

What reason does Sermon 515 give for why a regenerated Christian does not need the Law’s whip to avoid sin?

Spurgeon teaches that a believer’s motivation to shun sin comes from gratitude for God’s free grace rather than fear of legal punishment. He declares, "Think not, Sirs, that the Christian needs to be flogged to virtue by the whip of the Law!" and explains that the regenerated spirit “pants for” righteousness and, having been “Divinely forgiven,” the Christian feels compelled to love God and cannot continue in sin. Thus, the internal bond of gratitude is stronger than any external coercion.

meta.heading: [Sermon 515 — "The Sinner's Advocate"]
meta.passage:
Man has found out many inventions, but such arguments are so transparently abominable that few consciences are so dead as to tolerate them. Bad as human nature is, it seldom turns the goodness of God into an argument for rebelling against Him. As for souls renewed by Divine Grace, they never can be guilty of such infamy. The Believer in Jesus reasons in quite another fashion. Is God so good?--then I will not grieve Him. Is He so ready to forgive my trans-gressions?--then I will love Him, by His Grace, and offend no more. Gratitude has bands which are stronger than iron, although softer than silk.

Think not, Sirs, that the Christian needs to be flogged to virtue by the whip of the Law! Dream not that we hate sin merely because of the Hell which follows it! If there were no Heaven for the righteous, the sons of God would follow after goodness because their regenerated spirit pants for it. And if there were no Hell for the wicked, from the necessity of his new-born nature, the true Christian would strive to escape from all iniquity. Loved of God, we feel we must love Him in return. Richly, yes, Divinely forgiven, we feel that we cannot live any longer in sin. Since Jesus died to rid us from all uncleanness, we feel that we cannot crucify our Lord afresh, and put Him to an open shame.

We need no nobler or more cogent arguments to lead a man to thorough consecration to God's cause and detestation of all evil than those fetched from the Free Grace of God. And what if some men do pervert the doctrine? Do not wicked minds corrupt everything?

What reason does the sermon give for considering Marah better than Elim?

The sermon teaches that Marah is regarded as superior because, although it is initially bitter, it ultimately yields a greater spiritual benefit than the pleasant waters of Elim. It states that "Marah, though it is bitter, is also better" and that "there shall be no bitterness in it, but an unutterable sweetness which shall be ours through time and eternity!" This contrast highlights the belief that God's people receive more fruit from trials than from comforts, making the bitter experience at Marah more noteworthy than the sweet provision at Elim.

meta.heading: [Sermon 2301 — "Marah Better Than Elim"]
meta.passage:
I have found it true since then and you and I, if we are, indeed, the people of God, will find it true to the end, that Marah, though it is bitter, is also better. And albeit that we do not like it, yet in the end there shall be no bitterness in it, but an unutterable sweetness which shall be ours through time and eternity!

We have a long record about Marah, have we not? I have read you four verses concerning Marah. How many verses have we about Elim? Only one. Does Marah deserve to be talked about four times as much as Elim? Perhaps it does. Perhaps there is four times as much fruit to be obtained from the bitter waters of Marah than from the 12 springs of water, and 70 palm trees at Elim. Who knows? This I know, however, that we are very apt to talk more about our bitters than about our sweets--and that is a serious fault. It were well if we had fewer murmuring words for our sorrows and more songs of thanksgiving for our blessings. Yet Holy Writ seems, here, to speak after the manner of men, and to let us have the four verses for the trial, and the one verse for the delight! Still, as it speaks, also, after the manner of God, I gather that Marah is, after all, more noteworthy than Elim and, truly, there does come to God's people something better out of their troubles than out of their joys.

Certainly one thing is clear, Israel had no miracle at Elim. Wells and palm trees they had, but they had no miracle, there, no miraculous change of the bitter into the sweet.

What are the four aspects of a soul’s supplication described in the sermon, and why is confession emphasized as necessary?

The sermon teaches that a successful pleader’s soul is presented in four aspects: first, a soul confessing, as shown by the declaration “I am poor and needy.”; second, a soul pleading, when it makes a plea and adds, “Make haste unto me, O God!”; third, a soul in urgency, crying, “Make no tarrying.”; and fourth, a soul grasping God, expressed by the psalmist’s words, “Thou art my help and my deliverer.” In addition, the preacher stresses that “confession is absolutely needful to the sinner when he first seeks a Saviour,” asserting that peace cannot be obtained until one acknowledges transgression before the Lord.

meta.heading: [Sermon 1018 — "Pleading"]
meta.passage:
In our text we have the soul of a successful pleader under four aspects: we view, first, the soul confessing: "I am poor and needy." You have next, the soul pleading, for he makes a plea out of his poor condition, and adds, "Make haste unto me, O God!" You see, thirdly, a soul in it's urgency, for he cries, "Make haste," and he varies the expression but keeps the same idea: "Make no tarrying." And you have in the fourth and last view, a soul grasping God, for the psalmist puts it thus: "Thou art my help and my deliverer"; thus with both hands he lays hold upon His God, so as not to let Him go till a blessing is obtained.

To begin with, then, we see in this model of supplication, A SOUL CONFESSING. The wrestler strips before he enters upon the contest, and confession does the like for the man who is about to plead with God. A racer on the plains of prayer cannot hope to win, unless, by confession, repentance, and faith, he lays aside every weight of sin.

Now, let it be ever remembered that confession is absolutely needful to the sinner when he first seeks a Saviour. It is not possible for thee, O seeker, to obtain peace for thy troubled heart, till thou shalt have acknowledged thy transgression and thine iniquity before the Lord. Thou mayest do what thou wilt, ay, even attempt to believe in Jesus, but thou shalt find that the faith of God's elect is not in thee, unless thou art willing to make a full confession of thy transgression, and lay bare thy heart before God.

What warning does William Gouge give about a husband who constantly commands his wife?

William Gouge warns that a husband who habitually commands his wife, without allowing persuasion or invitation, will eventually exhaust his own authority. He likens such over‑use of authority to “a swag gerers sword, which cannot long rest in the sheath, but vpon euery small occasion is drawne forth,” and observes that “Thus as by trying to bend steele how farre it will goe, it oft breaketh; so by putting their authoritie to the vttermost triall, they oft lose all their authoritie.” The remedy, he notes, lies in the husband’s own hands.

According to Spurgeon in Sermon 1366, what happens when a person keeps silent about their spiritual sorrow?

Spurgeon teaches that unconfessed sorrow leads to a painful inner decay, noting that "When I kept silence," and did not pour out my sorrow when I ought to have confessed it, "my bones waxed old through my roaring all the day long." He urges believers to "Weep out the fullness of Your passionate grief" and to use the Psalms and David’s example as a mercy for expressing such grief.

meta.heading: [Sermon 1366 — "The Danger of Unconfessed Sin"]
meta.passage:
My child of sorrow, Weep out the fullness of Your passionate grief, And drown in tears The bitterness of lonely years." We shall now, however, think of spiritual sorrows and to these the same rule applies. "When I kept silence," and did not pour out my sorrow when I ought to have confessed it, "my bones waxed old through my roaring all the day long." Is it not a great mercy for us that we have the Book of Psalms and the life of such a man as David? Biographies of most people, nowadays, are like the portraits of a past generation when the art of flattery in oils was at its height. There is no greater cheat than a modem biography! It is not the man, at all, but what he might have been if he had not been something else! They give you a lock of his hair, or his wig, or his old coat, but seldom the man.

They make huge volumes out of a heap of his letters which ought to have been burned. And they copy little scraps of pictures which he used to draw for friends--and neither the letters nor the sketches ought ever to have been published. Like burglars, they break into a man's chamber and steal his hidden things. They hold up to the public eye what was meant for privacy, only, and expose the secrets of the man's heart and hearth. Things which the man would never have drawn or written if he had thought that they would meet the public eye are dragged forth and brought out as precious things, and so they are, but precious nonsense!

We have no biographers nowadays. When Boswell died, the greatest of all biographers died, and he was not far removed from a fool.

What does Edwards say about the nature of a legal spirit in those who profess humility?

Edwards observes that many who boast of their own vileness do so with a false, pharisaical affectation rather than genuine humility, and he warns that even those who denounce legalism may be secretly possessed by it. He explains that "A legal spirit is a more subtle thing than we imagine" and that it "lurks, and operates, and prevails in their hearts" even while they inveigh against it. Thus, unless a person is completely emptied of self‑righteousness, the legal spirit remains present in every form and shape.

What does Gill describe as the matter of satisfaction and how does Christ fulfill the law according to his doctrine?

Gill explains that the matter of satisfaction is ‘what that is which gives satisfaction to the justice of God; so that a sinner upon it, or in consideration of it, is acquitted and discharged.’ He argues that Christ accomplishes this by fulfilling the whole law in the place and stead of sinners. Gill notes that Christ voluntarily entered the covenant, saying, "Thy law is within my heart;" and that He came into the world ‘under it voluntarily, and became subject to it, for he came not to destroy it, but to fulfil it.’ Consequently, Christ is described as ‘the end of the law,’ having obeyed every precept perfectly and without sin, thereby providing the satisfaction required for justification.

How does the sermon explain the way holy anxiety can be misinterpreted as unbelief?

Spurgeon explains that the believer’s earnest concern for spiritual matters can be wrongly judged as a lack of faith. He observes that “Holy anxiety, when it broods over us, is often mistaken for unbelief,” and warns that such misinterpretation leads to suspicion of full assurance as presumption and to doubting joy for fear of pride. By highlighting this confusion, the preacher urges believers to recognize that genuine spiritual fervor, even when it feels like anxiety, is not a sign of unbelief but a sign of a living, sensitive soul.

meta.heading: [Sermon 1323 — "And Why Not?"]
meta.passage:
I have said unto my soul sometimes, "How heavy you are! How are you bowed down! How little do you rejoice in the Lord! It is sad that you should fall into this condition."

The period of heaviness has passed away and then I have chided my heart in another way, saying, "Soul, how careless and unfeeling you are! It were better for you if you were as heavy, now, as you were a little while ago, for then you were in earnest--then you were driven to mighty and prevailing prayer--but now you are steeped in lethargy! You have lost your fervency and are scarcely alive at all!" This stage has gone by and I have again had to look back and feel that when I thought myself insensible I was really very spiritual and sensitive--and that my fears of falling into carnal ease were sure proofs that I was carefully upon the watch. Thus are we delivered from carnal security by being made to see more beauty in past experiences than in those now passing over us.

Holy anxiety, when it broods over us, is often mistaken for unbelief. Full assurance is suspected to be presumption and joy is doubted and stinted for fear it should be pride and self-deception! When our spiritual spring is with us, we are fearful of its March winds and April showers. But when it is gone and we are parched with summer heat, we wish we had the winds and showers back again.

According to Downame, why can the regenerate part be confident of ultimate victory despite the apparent strength of the flesh?

Downame teaches that the regenerate part can be confident of ultimate victory because the spirit is "the Lords champion which goeth out in the name of the Lord to sight against his enemies" and is strengthened by the power of God, which is "insinit is vnresistable". In contrast, the flesh and its lusts are described as "the diuels souldier who is Gods enemie" and are limited by the finite power of Satan and the world, which are ultimately subject to God's might. Therefore, even though the flesh may seem strong and the conflict may involve many foils, the regenerate part shall "most certainely obtaine the victorie in the end".

What two personal qualities does Jesus claim for Himself in Sermon 265, and how does the preacher contrast one of them with a historical figure?

Spurgeon explains that Jesus declares Himself to be both "meek" and "lowly in heart," inviting sinners to come to Him because of this gentle character. He then contrasts Christ’s meekness with the ferocity of the false prophet Mahomet, noting that Mahomet’s strength lies in the fact that he is not meek.

meta.heading: [Sermon 265 — "The Meek and Lowly One"]
meta.passage:
"Come unto me and learn; for I am meek and lowly in heart." As much as to say, "I can teach, and you will not find it hard to learn of me." In fact, the subject of this morning's discourse is briefly this: the gentle, lovely character of Christ should be a high and powerful inducement to sinners to come to Christ. I intend so to use it: first of all, noticing the two qualities which Christ here claims for himself. He is "meek;" and then he is "lowly in heart;" and after we have observed these two things, I shall come to push the conclusion home. Come unto him, all ye that are labouring and are heavy laden; come unto him, and take his yoke upon you; for he is meek and lowly in heart.

First, then, I am to consider THE FIRST QUALITY WHICH JESUS CHRIST CLAIMS. He declares that he is "MEEK."

Christ is no egotist; he takes no praise to himself. If ever he utters a word in self-commendation, it is not with that object; it is with another design, namely that he may entice souls to come to him. Here, in order to exhibit this meekness, I shall have to speak of him in several ways.

First, Christ is meek, as opposed to the ferocity of spirit manifested by zealots and bigots. Take, for a prominent example of the opposite of meekness, the false prophet Mahomet. The strength of his cause lies in the fact, that he is not meek.

According to Flavel, does death break the covenant relationship between a believer and God?

Flavel teaches that death does not sever the covenant bond a believer has with God. He writes, "death puts an end to all other relations and bonds, but the bond of the covenant decays not in the grave," and he cites Romans 8:38‑39 to affirm that "death separates not the believer from the love of God." Thus, even in the grave the believer remains owned by the Lord and continues to enjoy divine love and providential care.

What does Owen say about the possibility of death providing relief to souls that are harassed by sinful passions?

Owen argues that death offers no respite for those whose souls are continually tormented by sinful passions. He observes that "In vain do such persons look for relief by death" and that any remaining present good will be taken from them, so that even a temporary freedom from bodily chains "will no way li(; in the balance against that confluence of evils which death will lot in upon them."

What does Sedgwick say about the proper remedy for a good man who is weakened by a vile lust?

Sedgwick teaches that for a good man who is "bowing under the actual power of some viler lust," comfort is not the appropriate remedy. He writes that "comfort is not his medicine, but repentance; comfort is not his first help, but godly sorrow." According to Sedgwick, the sinner must experience "godly sorrow" and allow his heart to be turned into "extreame loathing of thy sin" before any favorable response from God or conscience can be expected. Until the soul is thoroughly humbled and its wickedness is the sinner will not receive a good look from God or any encouraging word from conscience.

What does Herbert say about the effect of omitting an additionary prayer on a believer’s spiritual state?

Herbert teaches that omission of an additionary prayer should not disturb the believer, because such prayers are "not necessary; taken in, not commanded." He explains that when a godly person misses a voluntary prayer due to an interruption, Satan may try to increase his perplexity, but the parson’s distinction reassures the Christian that God, as a gracious Father, "more accepts a common course of devotion, then dislikes an occasionall interruption." Therefore, the believer can proceed cheerfully without feeling guilty for the missed optional prayer.

meta.heading: [Herbert — Country Parson]
meta.passage:
Besides this, the Godly have ever added some houres of prayer,
 as at nine, or at three, or at midnight, or as they think fit, & see
 cause, or rather as Gods spirit leads them. But these prayers are not
 necessary, but additionary. Now it so happens, that the godly
 petitioner upon some emergent interruption in the day, or by
 over-sleeping himself at night, omits his additionary prayer. Upon this
 his mind begins to be perplexed, and troubled, and Satan, who knows the
 exigent, blows the fire, endeavouring to disorder the Christian, and
 put him out of his station, and to inlarge the perplexity, untill it

 wel in trouble, as in calmness. Here the Parson interposeth with his
 distinction, and shews the perplexed Christian, that this prayer being
 additionary, not necessary; taken in, not commanded, the omission
 thereof upon just occasion ought by no means to trouble him. God knows

 accepts a common course of devotion, then dislikes an occasionall
 interruption. And of this he is so to assure himself, as to admit no
 scruple, but to go on as cheerfully, as if he had not been interrupted.
 By this it is evident, that the distinction is of singular use and
 comfort, especially to pious minds, which are ever tender, and

What does the first message described in the sermon promise to the 'daughter of Zion'?

The sermon teaches that the first message is one of comfort, declaring that the punishment for sin has been completed and that the daughter of Zion will be freed from future captivity. It states, "The punishment of thine iniquity is accomplished, O daughter of Zion; he will no more carry thee away into captivity."

meta.heading: [Sermon 480 — "A Message from God for Thee"]
meta.passage:
I say not alone, as did the blind prophet of old, "Come in, thou wife of Jeroboam; for I am sent to thee with heavy tidings;" but I have also to say, "Come in thou blessed of the Lord, wherefore standest thou without." According to the persons I address, my message will be as pleasant as ever was brought by those whose feet were beautiful upon the mountains because they published good tidings of great joy, or as dreadful as that which Daniel bore to the trembling monarch in the day when his kingdom was divided and given to the Medes and Persians.

Our two messages we will try to deliver in their order; we shall then want your attention and patience for a minute while we answer the question--Why the difference? and then we will press upon each character the force of the message, that each may be led to believe what is addressed to him.

Our FIRST MESSAGE IS ONE OF COMFORT. "The punishment of thine iniquity is accomplished, O daughter of Zion; he will no more carry thee away into captivity."

We find, at the outset, a joyous fact.

According to Hodge, why did Paul send a brother to take charge of the contributions in connection with the apostle?

Hodge explains that Paul was “determined to avoid all occasion of reproach, and therefore he associated others with himself in the charge of the money,” and so he sent a brother who “had not only the approbation of the churches, but had been chosen for the very purpose of taking charge of the contributions in connection with the apostle.” This arrangement was intended to ensure fairness and transparency in the collection, reflecting the apostle’s wish for “some approximation to equality among Christians.”

What are the first two of the six burdens that Rutherford lists in his letter?

Rutherford enumerates his burdens by first stating, "I am not in the vineyard as others are; it may be, because Christ thinketh me a withered tree, not worth its room." This expresses his sense of spiritual barrenness and exclusion from the work of the Lord. His second burden is a lament for the church, which he calls "my harlot-mother, this apostate kirk," and he warns that "Woe, woe, woe is coming upon" it, anticipating great distress for the body of believers.

How does the sermon describe the relationship between Christ and spiritual nourishment?

The sermon teaches that Christ functions as the believer's essential spiritual sustenance, comparing Him to physical food that keeps the body alive. It declares that "THE FLESH OF CHRIST IS MEAT INDEED--SPIRITUAL MEAT," emphasizing that just as meat sustains the flesh, Christ sustains the soul. Without this daily spiritual meat, the believer would "pine, we languish, we sicken, we die" and ultimately fall into apostasy.

meta.heading: [Sermon 3424 — "Meat Indeed, and Drink Indeed"]
meta.passage:
Taking the words as they stand, our first point will be that--

THE FLESH OF CHRIST IS MEAT INDEED--SPIRITUAL MEAT.

The likeness is emphatic--it is "meat indeed." I t is like meat because meat, or food, sustains the body. The body could not be kept in vigor ordinarily or without a miracle, except by the use of food. We pine, we languish, we sicken, we die without bread! So the soul without Jesus, supposing it to be alive, must soon sicken, pine, be famished and decay. You, O Believer, with all your strength would be weak as water at this moment if Jesus were not now your present support! All your past experience would go for nothing if you had not now a present Christ to stay your hopes upon. It would be only a matter of time with you--you would before long sink into the corruption of an open apostasy. Like a man shut up in a dungeon and deprived of food who drags out for a few days, a most painful existence and, at the last, expires and becomes carrion, so must it be with you. Unless Jesus Christ is your daily meat, you would go back to the carnal elements of the world and become corrupt and depraved as others are! Christ is the only true sustenance of the quickened soul. But, mark you, let a man eat what meat he may, it does not always so sustain him but that he is not sometimes weak and stretched upon the bed of languishing. It cannot so sustain him but that before long he must be carried to his grave.

Why does Calvin say Paul swears an oath in the preface to his letter to the Romans?

Calvin explains that Paul anticipates the widespread suspicion that he was a sworn enemy of his own nation and that he had taught the Jews to forsake Moses, so he adds a preface to prepare his readers and to clear himself of that false accusation. To make his affirmation credible against the existing prejudice, Paul "declares by an oath that he speaks the truth," thereby removing the obstacle of Jewish unbelief and securing the course of the gospel.

meta.heading: [Calvin — Commentary Romans]
meta.passage:
It so happened in this way, -- Having finished the doctrine he
 discussed, he turned his attention to the Jews, and being astonished at
 their unbelief as at something monstrous, he burst forth into this
 sudden protestation, in the same way as though it was a subject which
 he had previously handled; for there was no one to whom this thought
 would not of itself immediately occur, -- "If this be the doctrine of
 the law and the Prophets, how comes it that the Jews so pertinaciously
 reject it?" And further, it was everywhere known, that all that he had
 hitherto spoken of the law of Moses, and of the grace of Christ, was
 more disliked by the Jews, than that the faith of the Gentiles should
 be assisted by their consent. It was therefore necessary to remove this
 obstacle, lest it should impede the course of the gospel.

 most that Paul was, as it were, a sworn enemy to his own nation, and as
 it was suspected somewhat even by the household of faith, as though he
 had taught them to forsake Moses, he adopts a preface to prepare the
 minds of his readers, before he proceeds to his subject, and in this
 preface he frees himself from the false suspicion of evil will towards
 the Jews. And as the matter was not unworthy of an oath, and as he
 perceived that his affirmation would hardly be otherwise believed
 against a prejudice already entertained, he declares by an oath that he
 speaks the truth.

What does the sermon say about God's ability to suffer or die?

Spurgeon argues that God is incapable of suffering or death, stating that "God cannot die!" and that "God is incapable of suffering." He explains that because God is impassive and cannot cease to exist, any language suggesting divine death is merely anthropomorphic. The sermon further clarifies that while Christ, being "very God of very God," possessed all divine attributes and could not suffer, He died in His human nature, "as Man that He gave up the ghost." Thus, the death on the cross pertains to Christ’s humanity, not to the immutable nature of God.

meta.heading: [Sermon 2656 — "The Death of Christ for His People"]
meta.passage:
If I were to tell you that God died for us, although I might be telling you the truth and you might possibly not misunderstand what I meant, yet I would be, at the same time, uttering an error. God cannot die! It is, of course, impossible, from His very Nature, that He could even for a moment cease to exist! God is incapable of suffering. It is true that we sometimes use words to express emotions on the part of God but, then, we speak after the manner of men. He is impassive. He cannot suffer. It is not possible for Him to endure anything, much less, then, is it possible for Him to suffer death. Yet we are told, in the verse from which our text is taken, "Hereby perceive we the love of God." You notice that the words, "of God," are inserted by the translators. They are in italics because they are not in the original. A better translation would be, "Hereby perceive we love." But when we read, "of God," it might lead the ignorant to fancy that God could die, whereas God could not.

We must always understand and constantly remember that our Lord Jesus Christ was "very God of very God" and that, as God, He had all the attributes of the Most High and could not, therefore, be capable either of suffering or death. But then He was also Man, "Man of the substance of His mother." Man, just like ourselves, sin alone excepted. And the Lord Jesus died not as God--it was as Man that He gave up the ghost. As Man, He was nailed to the Cross. As God, He was in Heaven, even when His body was in the tomb.

According to the sermon, what warning does the fate of Moab give to the unconverted and how is prosperity described as a spiritual danger?

Spurgeon teaches that the prosperity of Moab is a warning of sudden divine judgment, stating that "the day shall come when God shall shake this undisturbed liquor, when He shall send wandering bands of Chaldeans that shall waste the country so that the bottles shall be broken and the vessels shall be emptied and the proud prosperity of Moab shall end in utter desolation." He further warns that a fire will arise from Heshbon and Sihon, and that the lament "Woe be unto you, O Moab! The people of Chemosh perish: for your sons are taken captive, and your daughters captives" illustrates the swift destruction that follows complacent wealth. Spurgeon emphasizes that this mischief is common among the ungodly and also a frequent danger to the most godly, urging the unconverted, godless, prayerless, and christless to avoid becoming like Moab.

meta.heading: [Sermon 761 — "The Shrill Trumpet of Admonition"]
meta.passage:
"But," he says, "the day shall come when God shall shake this undisturbed liquor, when He shall send wandering bands of Chaldeans that shall waste the country so that the bottles shall be broken and the vessels shall be emptied and the proud prosperity of Moab shall end in utter desolation."

The unusual repose of Moab had been the envy of the people of Israel, but they might well cease to envy when they understood how suddenly a fire should come forth out of Heshbon, and a flame from the midst of Sihon and devour the corner of Moab--and how soon the howling should be heard, "Woe be unto you, O Moab! The people of Chemosh perish: for your sons are taken captive, and your daughters captives." The fact that continued prosperity breeds carnal security is not only proved by the instance of Moab, but is lamentably confirmed in the history of others.

In the first place, this is the common mischief of ungodly men. In the second place, this is the frequent danger of the most godly.

I shall first speak to THE UNCONVERTED, THE GODLESS, THE PRAYERLESS, THE CHRISTLESS. Many of you, though not all, become like Moab. At ease from your youth you are not emptied from vessel to vessel but settled upon your lees, and therefore you grow careless and heedless. This is so common a mischief among the ungodly that the whole world was in this condition immediately before the great deluge which destroyed the ancient race.

What future blessings does Baxter describe for the saints in the new earth?

Baxter teaches that the saints will enjoy an everlasting state of joy in the new creation, where all former sorrows are erased. He envisions that they will "drink then of the river of pleasure, the streams whereof make glad the city of God" and that "the former shall not be remembered." In this renewed Jerusalem there will be no more weeping or crying, no infants or old men who have not filled their days, and the people of God will rejoice forever in the presence of the Lord.

What does Owen identify as the principal preparatory means for the continuance and increase of the church?

Owen explains that the chief preparatory means for the church’s continuance and increase is the proclamation of Scripture that leads to conviction, illumination, and conversion of sinners, thereby making them "living stones in this spiritual building, and members of the mystical body of Christ." He emphasizes that this preaching occurs ordinarily in the assemblies of the church, reaching those who come to hear the word as appointed by Christ.

What does the Ames passage identify as the highest distinction between a good work and sin?

Ames explains that the highest distinction lies in the motive of reward: a good work is performed expecting happiness as a reward, while sin lacks that expectation and results in extreme evil. He states, "the proper and highest difference of a good work and sinne doth flow, namely in that a good worke is an operation expecting happinesse of another by way of reward". This distinction also gives rise to conscience as the judgment of the creature.

What does Dabney say about the possibility of Christ possessing infinite attributes such as omnipotence?

Dabney argues that a finite nature cannot receive infinite endowments, so Christ cannot possess attributes that are truly infinite. He writes that “it is in the nature of things simply impossible that a finite nature should receive infinite endowments,” and emphasizes that “Even Omnipotence cannot make a part to contain the whole.” Accordingly, Dabney rejects the idea that Christ shares the full divine omnipotence.

How does the author of 'Vestiges of Creation' use the development of the human fetus to argue for a progressive view of animal orders?

The author of 'Vestiges of Creation' argues that the stages of fetal development illustrate a natural progression of complexity among animal groups, suggesting that each higher order recapitulates the forms of lower ones. He points out that "the human foetus, for example, assuming in succession the peculiarities of structure of the reptile, of the fish, of the bird, and of man," thereby claiming that humanity is a more fully developed reptile and that the differences among animal orders are merely stages in an unfolding series of life.

According to Cotton, what actions can the churches take when an errant church refuses to heed correction?

Cotton teaches that after giving due notice, the surrounding churches may convene, conduct a judicious enquiry, and by the word of God "confute and condemne such errours in doctrine or practice". If the offending church still does not repent, the churches have the authority to "withdraw from them the right hand of fellowship, and no longer to hold them in communion of Saints, till they approve their repentance". This disciplinary measure is presented as a biblical remedy to prevent the spread of heresy and sin, while affirming that such ecclesiastical actions do not infringe upon civil authority.

What does Manton describe as the 'former work' that forms the foundation of all Christian duties?

Manton teaches that the first and foundational task for believers is to secure a firm belief in the future hopes of Christianity. He writes, "there is a former work, which is the foundation of all, and that is, to settle the soul in a sound belief of the things to come, and have the hopes of Christianity evidenced to us". By establishing this conviction, the mind is satisfied, leading to greater awe in practice and preventing the "privy atheism" that weakens grace.

According to the sermon, how is the Roman Catholic Church characterized and what judgment is promised for it?

Spurgeon teaches that the Roman Catholic Church is portrayed as the "mother of harlots and abominations of the earth" and that God will bring a terrible judgment upon it on the Last Day, destroying it utterly.

meta.heading: [Sermon 3144 — "The True Sayings of God"]
meta.passage:
In the old Jewish time, idolatry was called spiritual harlotry--and there are millions of idolaters daily bowing down before images, rags and bones that ought long ago to have been buried in the earth. The Church of Rome seems to have gathered up all the relics of the idolatries of other ages and then to have capped them by saying that a substance which is only bread before the "priest" consecrates it, becomes God afterwards and then the idolater eats his god--a monstrous piece of blasphemy and superstition unworthy of Dahomey itself! That is the harlot church which God will surely judge. And when He does, terrible will be that judgment! Among the tremendous things of the Last Day will be the total overthrow and utter destruction of this "mother of harlots and abominations of the earth." Come you out from her, O you people, lest you be partakers of her plagues, for terrible will her plagues be in the day when the Lord shall avenge upon her the blood of all His saints and martyrs whom she has slain. This, then, is one of "the true sayings of God."

The next true saying is concerning the glorious and universal reign of the great God. For John "heard, as it were, the voice of a great multitude, and as the voice of many waters, and as the voice of mighty thunders saying, Alleluia: for the Lord God omnipotent reigns." There has been a long war between God and idols of various names. Among the ancient idols were Baal and Ashtaroth, and Dagon--but all had to bow down before Jehovah. Then Jupiter, and Saturn, and Venus and Mars were worshipped as deities by the heathen.

How does Shedd argue that the soul itself proves the existence of the true God?

Shedd maintains that the soul, even while imprisoned in the body and weakened by lusts and passions, recovers its sober condition and instinctively calls upon the true God, demonstrating an innate witness to divine existence. He notes that “Great God,” “Good God,” and “God grant,” are words in every mouth, showing that the human spirit looks upward to heaven rather than to pagan idols. By citing the testimony of the soul and the monotheistic tendencies found among pagan philosophers, Shedd concludes that the divine existence is evident from the soul’s own testimony.

What analogy does Reynolds use to describe the premature development of the mind in his Treatise of the Passions?

Reynolds likens the premature development of the mind to early blossoms that burst forth before their proper season, suffering damage from subsequent weather. He writes that “the too Early Conceptions and Issues of them doe usu ally proove but weake and unusefull” and compares them to “those ven turous Blossoms, whose over-hastie obe dience to the Early Spring doth anticipate their proper season, and put forth too soone, doe afterwards for their former boldnesse suffer from the injury of seve rer weather.” This vivid image illustrates his view that intellectual maturity should not be forced ahead of its natural timing.

What does Spurgeon mean by the instruction ‘gird up the loins of your mind’ in Sermon 2649?

Spurgeon teaches that the apostolic command to “gird up the loins of your mind” is a vivid metaphor urging believers to tighten the loose and flowing thoughts that surround their intellect, just as an Eastern robe must be well‑girded before one can move freely. He explains that without such mental preparation the believer becomes an “encumbrance and a hindrance,” and he warns that many professing Christians are “very lax even in matters of morality.” By binding the mind tightly, the Christian is prepared for active spiritual exercise and for the grace that will be revealed at Christ’s coming. "Therefore gird up the loins of your mind, be sober, and hope to the end for the Grace that is to be brought unto you at the revelation of Jesus Christ."

meta.heading: [Sermon 2649 — "Girded for the Work"]
meta.passage:
What would God have me do as the result of receiving such teaching as this?" From what Peter had already said, like a true logician, he draws a wise inference and says, "Therefore gird up the loins of your mind, be sober, and hope to the end for the Grace that is to be brought unto you at the revelation of Jesus Christ."

We shall only have time to consider the first few words of the Apostle's exhortation, "Therefore gird up the loins of your mind." And, concerning them, we will ask three questions, First, What are we to do? Secondly, Why are we to do it? And, thirdly, How are we to do it?

First, let us enquire, WHAT ARE WE TO DO? "Gird up the loins of your mind."

The metaphor used by Peter is a very simple one. The garments of the Easterns, as you know, are not like ours, but are long flowing robes and, unless the raiment is well gird about the wearer, there is little or nothing that he can do in the way of active exercise. In a spiritual sense, the injunction, "Gird up the loins of your mind," is a very proper one to be addressed to those of us who have various loose and flowing things which are almost as natural to us as garments are to the body. They must be gird about us very tightly or else they will become an encumbrance and a hindrance.

We may possibly understand what is meant by our text if we, first, consider the opposite condition. Some persons are notorious for their laxity--whatever they have about them is very loosely attached to them. I am grieved to say that there are some professing Christians who are very lax even in matters of morality.

According to Sibbes, what power will raise believers at the resurrection?

Sibbes teaches that the resurrection will be effected solely by the power of Christ, not by any natural force, as he affirms "by the power of Christ ; no power else can do it." He explains that this divine power will raise the godly with boldness, joy, and ravishment, while the wicked will rise with fear, shame, and astonishment. Moreover, Sibbes outlines three uses of this truth: first, to magnify and rely upon this mighty power; second, to labor to feel the power of Christ in this life; and third, to trust that the Lord will raise believers out of all troubles.

Why does the sermon say the Scriptures were especially dear to David?

Spurgeon explains that David valued the Scriptures because they warned him against evil—"by them Your servant is warned."—and because obedience to them brought a great reward—"and in keeping them there is great reward." The sermon stresses that the Bible is perfectly sized and adapted for every person, serving as a constant guide that saves us from many mistakes and evil.

meta.heading: [Sermon 2775 — "David Warned and Rewarded"]
meta.passage:
We have a Bible which is large enough to be a perfect library and which is also so compact that we can carry it about with us wherever we go! It is exactly the right size and it is just right in all other respects. It is just adapted to every individual in the world and it is also the most fit Book for any nation to use as an everyday guide as to its morals, its laws and its conduct in relation to both God and men.

There are two things mentioned in the text which made the Scriptures very dear to David. The first is that they had warned him against evil--"by them Your servant is warned." And the second is that obedience to the Scriptures had brought him a great reward--"and in keeping them there is great reward."

First, then, THE SCRIPTURES HAD WARNED DAVID AGAINST EVIL.

We are so dull and so foolish that unless we are taught of God the Holy Spirit, we really know nothing as we ought to know it. Yet we are so headstrong and so obstinate that if we are not Divinely checked, we run with heedless impetuosity into all manner of evil. We need to be goaded on to everything that is good, but we need to be held in with a tight rein, or we shall plunge into many things that are evil. Even when we do not willfully choose the wrong, we seem to run into it by a sort of natural tendency--and we find ourselves bogged down before we know where we are. If, however, the Scripture is made to be our constant companion and guide, we shall be saved from many mistakes into which, otherwise, we are sure to fall.

What does Burgess say about the way God tests a believer’s heart and how the gold‑refining image illustrates that testing?

Burgess teaches that God’s testing of believers is meant to reveal the purity of their hearts, much as a refiner purifies gold. He points to the biblical language that a believer’s heart is examined: "Thou hast proved my heart, thou hast tryed me, and hast found nothing;" and he links this to the promise that "When he hath tryed me, I shall come out like Gold." The purpose of such testing, according to Burgess, is to demonstrate a love and willingness to have one’s heart searched by God, which becomes a "great bulwark in times of sad afflictions." He further explains that the primary means by which God tries people is through His Word, which acts as light that exposes and refines, just as the Scriptures are likened to the Sun that shines light on all things. This refining process validates true grace and exposes falsehood, just as false weights are abominable to the Lord.

According to Spurgeon in this sermon, how are believers described before God’s deliverance?

Spurgeon teaches that every person in his unrenewed state is a slave, likening believers to the Israelites in Egypt, and that only by God’s power can they be delivered. He declares that the Lord’s word is "Thus says the Lord, let My people go, that they may serve Me." This imperial mandate reveals the divine call to freedom from bondage. Spurgeon warns that without God’s intervention, any human effort to rebel would be crushed by the "tremendous power of that great monarch of Egypt."

meta.heading: [Sermon 322 — "A Divine Challenge!"]
meta.passage:
In fact, the Word which Jehovah is now speaking to the entire world with the solemn authority of an imperial mandate is this—"Thus says the Lord, let My people go, that they may serve Me."

It will be necessary in addressing you this evening, to recall to your minds the position which the Israelites held in Egypt. It is a type of the position of all the Lord's people before the Most High God, who with a high hand and an outstretched arm brings them out of their bondage. The people of the Lord are slaves. Though their names are in His book, yet they are slaves, engaged like Israel of old in labors that savor more of earthly than of heavenly things—brick-makers, building houses not for themselves, for they find no city to dwell in. They are toiling and laboring here as unwilling servants, thinking, perhaps, they shall receive goodly wages, but they receive no wages, except the whip upon their shoulders. Every man in his unrenewed state is a slave. Even God's people are slaves as well as others, till they hear the trumpet of jubilee and at the Word and by the power of God are brought forth out of the place of their slavery. We are slaves—slaves to a power which we can never overcome by our own unassisted strength. If all the inhabitants of Goshen—the Israelites, I mean—had concerted measures to rebel against Pharaoh and had said, "We will be free"—in but a few hours, the tremendous power of that great monarch of Egypt would have crushed out the last spark of hope.

According to Flavel, how should ministers and laypeople respect each other's distinct callings within the church?

Flavel teaches that the church is to be a well‑ordered household where each person keeps his proper station. He stresses that “Ministers would not invade the civil callings of the people, nor the people the sacred calling of the ministry ; but all things would move ordinately secundum, sub et supra.” Thus pastors are to feed and govern the flock while laypeople attend to their secular duties, and neither group should usurp the other’s role.

What does the Westminster Catechisms of 1756 say about the character of Christian hope?

The Westminster Catechisms of 1756 explain that true Christian hope is a confident expectation of the unseen redemption of the body, not a hope based on visible evidence. As the catechism notes, "we are saved by hope: but hope that is seen, is not hope". Hence believers are to wait patiently for the adoption and redemption that God promises, looking forward to the Lord’s return with watchful hearts.

What mutual duties does William Gouge assign to husbands and wives in marriage?

William Gouge teaches that the marital relationship is a mutual duty in which each spouse is to love, cherish, and support the other through all circumstances. He cites the Apostle’s instruction that "No man hateth his owne flesh, but nourisheth and cherisheth it," applying it specifically to husbands and extending it to wives as well. Gouge stresses that this duty covers both prosperity and adversity, health and sickness, and requires spouses to "putting their shoulders vnder one anothers burden, and helping to ease one another as much as they can."
