According to Spurgeon, how does Jesus respond to the prayers of sinners who feel distant from Him?

Spurgeon teaches that Jesus, though exalted as King of Kings, retains the same compassionate heart toward sinners that He displayed on earth, and He is ever ready to hear their cries. He emphasizes that even the most despondent believer can approach the Mercy Seat, because "He will stop to give heed to the requests of blind beggars" and will attend to the sighs, tears, and groans of the contrite. Thus, Spurgeon assures that no prayer is too feeble or too sinful to reach the Lord’s merciful ear.

meta.heading: [Sermon 3537 — "A Definite Challenge for Definite Prayer"]
meta.passage:
Though our Lord Jesus Christ is at this moment King of Kings and Lord of Lords, and inconceivably glorious, though hosts of angels count it their highest delight to do His bidding, yet He bears in Heaven the same heart towards sinners which He had on earth! Amidst the thunders of the everlasting hallelujahs, He can detect the sighs of the prisoners, the complaints of the sufferers and the groans of the contrite. He will stop to give heed to the requests of blind beggars and, in His pity, He will relieve their distress. Should not this encourage those of you who are seeking Him? Whatever Satan may suggest to the contrary, take this passage of God's Word for cheer! He did hear the blind man's cry when He was upon earth and He will hear you, now that He is in Heaven! And you, backsliding child of God, difficult as you may find it to pray, if enabled to vent your griefs, your sighs shall be heard, your tears shall be seen and you shall certainly have an audience from Him who delights in mercy! There are times even with those who live nearest to God, when they fall into despondencies and imagine that their voice is shut out from Heaven's gate, but it is not so! When I cannot come to God as a saint, what a mercy it is that I may come to Him as a sinner! And if I have lost all my evidences, what a blessing it is that I need not stop to find them, that I may go to the Mercy Seat without any!--

"Just as I am without one plea, But that His blood was shed for me."

When reduced to the utmost beggary as to internal Grace.

What next step does Spurgeon say believers must take after they have entered into rest, according to Sermon 2086?

Spurgeon teaches that entering into rest is only the beginning; believers must respond to Christ’s invitation to discipleship. He urges them to "Take My yoke upon you and learn of Me: and you shall find rest unto your souls," indicating that true, lasting rest is discovered through willing service and obedience to Christ’s yoke. By taking this step, believers move from a mere pardon of sin to a deeper, holistic salvation that includes being saved to holiness and possessing the inheritance promised in Christ.

meta.heading: [Sermon 2086 — "Taking Possession Of Our Inheritance"]
meta.passage:
I want the Lord's people so to persevere in their seeking, by Divine strength, that they may get out of the great and terrible wilderness and come to Mount Zion and the heavenly Jerusalem and enter into their heritage, according to that word, "We which have believed do enter into rest."

Our friends have come as far as that first verse of our Lord's invitation, "Come unto Me, all you that labor and are heavy laden and I will give you rest." And they have a measure of that rest which comes of pardoned sin and confidence in Jesus. The pity is that they have not advanced to His next word of exhortation, "Take My yoke upon you and learn of Me: and you shall find rest unto your souls." This is a rest discovered and enjoyed through willing service--"You shall find rest unto your souls." Many people are saved in one sense but in another sense they are seeking salvation.

Oh that we may come to be saved in every sense--may salvation be ours in the broadest, widest, deepest, highest meaning of that blessed word! May we not only be saved from but saved to! Saved from sin--that makes us safe. Saved to holiness--that makes us happy. May we realize our completeness in Christ this day and cease from the wanderings of fear! It is time that we took possession of that goodly heritage which the Lord has made our own, for in Christ Jesus "we have obtained an inheritance" and have the earnest of it in our possession of the Spirit of God.

What reason does Spurgeon give in Sermon 3463 for why some people do not believe even when truth is plain?

Spurgeon teaches that moral character, especially pride and a love of grandiloquent titles, blinds people to the truth. He argues that the Scribes and Pharisees were "prejudiced" and thought they possessed "the key of knowledge," which made them unable to receive Christ’s teaching, while even publicans and harlots could hear and rejoice. Thus, he concludes that "IT IS NOT BECAUSE A TRUTH IS PLAIN THAT, THEREFORE, ALL MEN SEE IT."

meta.heading: [Sermon 3463 — "Why Men Do Not Believe"]
meta.passage:
You gentlemen are so given to complimentary phrases and to grandiloquent titles, that there was no likelihood that you would listen to a Man who came with Truth on His lips, and still further, in His heart." Perhaps there could be nothing more clear than that the position which the Scribes and Pharisees occupied was most dangerous. They were prejudiced. They considered that they had the key of knowledge. They already knew by far, too much to be taught anything more and, consequently, while publicans and harlots heard Christ and rejoiced to listen to Him, out of all those who were continually caviling and finding fault, how few ever won the blessing!

Now this is an illustration of a general rule upon which I wish to speak tonight. The moral character has a great effect upon the faith. These men, through being proud, stilted and fond of titles, were unable to believe in Christ--but there are other faults more common than these which effectually prevent men from becoming the disciples of our blessed Master. Of some of these I intend to speak this evening. And when I have done so, I shall have a few words to address to the individuals here who cannot believe in Christ because there is a something within their hearts that very effectually prevents their coming to the faith of God's elect. First, then, it is very clear that--

IT IS NOT BECAUSE A TRUTH IS PLAIN THAT, THEREFORE, ALL MEN SEE IT.

According to the Institutes Beveridge, what erroneous scriptural arguments are presented for the use of images in worship?

The Institutes records that advocates of images cite a series of strained interpretations, for example they claim that because "Lord, I have loved the beauty of thy house." images are therefore appropriate, and they also argue that "No man, when he hath lighted a candle, putteth it under a bushel." justifies placing images on altars. The work further notes that such interpreters twist passages like "The light of thy countenance, O Lord, has shone upon us" to argue for the utility of looking at images, and even appeal to the statement that "God created man in his own image," to suggest that images ought to be used. Ultimately, the Institutes concludes that these arguments are so extreme that "it is painful even to quote them."

What specific tragedies does the sermon say caused the Patriarch’s deep sorrow?

Spurgeon explains that the Patriarch’s anguish stemmed from a succession of calamities: he “had lost all his property,” his and then he was “smitten from head to foot with boils.” These compounded losses illustrate why the man questioned the purpose of divine light amid such suffering.

meta.heading: [Sermon 2666 — "The Sorrowful Man's Question"]
meta.passage:
"Why is light given to a man whose way is hidden, and whom God has hedged in?" His case was so sad and so trying that life itself became irksome to him. I suppose that by, "light," here, he means the power to see the Light of God, the life which lives in the light. "Why," he asked in his agony, "is that continued to a man when God has filled him with sorrow upon sorrow?" The verses preceding our text are to the same effect--"Therefore is light given to him that is in misery, and life unto the bitter in soul which long for death, but it comes not; and dig for it more than for hidden treasures; which rejoice exceedingly and are glad when they can find the grave."

The Patriarch was weary of living and, perhaps, we shall not wonder so much at his pitiful lamentation if we remember the extreme distress into which he had been brought. He had lost all his property. Stroke by stroke all his wealth had been taken away from him. He might have borne that if it had been his only loss, but close upon the heels of it had come sore bereavement. His happy children, for whom he daily cared and whom he had tenderly loved, were all destroyed in a moment--while they were feasting in the house of one of their brothers. The calamity seemed all the greater because it came in the very midst of their joys. Then, as if that was not trial enough, Job was, himself, smitten from head to foot with boils. If you have ever seen a person in that condition, I am sure that you must pity him. There is a dear friend of ours, now with God, whom I visited when he was in much the same state as that.

What does Gill say about how the resurrection of the saints affected the disciples' hope for the restoration of the kingdom?

Gill explains that the resurrection of many of the saints, together with Christ’s own rising, caused the disciples to believe that the long‑awaited restoration of the kingdom was now imminent. He notes that they "might hope that this was the time the kingdom would be restored," because they linked the personal reign of Christ with the resurrection of the just. Thus, the resurrection served as the catalyst that revived their expectation that the Messiah would now restore the kingdom to Israel.

meta.passage:
"Lord, wilt thou at this time restore the kingdom
 unto Israel?" The sceptre, according to ancient prophecy, was now
 departed from Judah, and Judea was become a province to the Roman
 empire; now the Jews had a notion, that when the Messiah came, he would
 restore the kingdom, and redeem them from the Roman yoke, and make them
 a happy people, as to temporal things; and with this notion, the
 disciples themselves were tinctured; and as they believed that Jesus
 was the Messiah, they had raised expectations of this matter; but when
 he was dead, their hopes seem to be almost quite gone (Luke 24:21), but
 Christ being raised from the dead, their hopes revived: and it was a
 notion that prevailed with the Jews, and does to this day, that the
 coming of the king Messiah, to deliver them, and the resurrection of
 the dead, will be at the same time: and, indeed, Christ's personal
 reign will take place after the resurrection of the just. And now there
 having been a resurrection of many of the saints (Matthew 27:52, 53),
 and especially Christ himself being risen, and also had spoken to his
 disciples of things pertaining to the kingdom of God (Matthew 27:3),
 they might hope that this was the time the kingdom would be restored.

What does Greenham say will happen when believers lack true joy in their worship and sacraments?

Greenham warns that without true joy worship becomes hypocritical and believers become weary and ready to hear other doctrines. He asks, "will they not begin to be wearie? nay will they not be as readie to heare any other doctrine?" Thus the lack of joy leads to hypocrisy, weariness, and openness to false teaching.

What does Gill say about the fate of the law in relation to the biblical statements that heaven and earth will pass away?

Gill teaches that the Scriptures affirm that the moral law will never be nullified, even though the created order is temporary. He notes that the first of those scriptures only says, "till heaven and earth pass", which will never be; and so not one jot or tittle of the law shall pass till all be fulfilled. Thus, while "heaven and earth shall pass away", the law endures until its ultimate fulfillment, and the passing of the world refers only to the temporary fashion and lusts of the age, not to the divine moral decree.

meta.heading: [Systematic — Gill Body Of Doctrinal Divinity]
meta.passage:
The first of those scriptures
 only says, "till heaven and earth pass", which will never be; and so
 not one jot or tittle of the law shall pass till all be fulfilled: the
 other indeed asserts, that "heaven and earth shall pass away"; but then
 the sense may be only comparatively, that sooner shall heaven and earth
 pass away, as they never shall, than that "Christ's words shall pass
 away": the last of them refers to the fashion of the world, and the
 lusts in it, which shall pass away, and have no place in the new earth;
 in which, not worldly and sinful lusts, only righteousness shall dwell.
 All such passages of scripture, likewise, which speak of "the end of
 the world", are brought into this argument: but these, some of them,
 have only reference to the end of the Jewish state: as 1 Corinthians
 10:11 and Hebrews 9:26 and others only refer to the present state of
 things in the world; but not to the destruction of it; as Matthew 28:20
 and such passages which only respect the mutability of the things of
 this world, and the temporary enjoyment of them, can be of no use in
 this controversy; as Hebrews 13:14 and 2 Corinthians 4:18.

What internal actions of God does Ambrose describe as common to the three persons of the Trinity?

Ambrose teaches that the three persons share internal actions of communication, specifically that they possess, glorify, and delight in one another. He explains that the Father remains with the Son, the Son with the Father, and the Holy Ghost in, "the Father remaining with the Son, the Son with the Father, and the Holy Ghost in, P ov. 8.22 John 1.1 John 14.10". He further notes that each glorifies the other, as reflected in the prayer, "And now, O Father, glorifie thou me with thine own self, with the glory which I had with thee before the world was." Finally, Ambrose says that each delights in the other, describing the Son as daily the Father's delight.

meta.heading: [Ambrose — Looking Unto Jesus]
meta.passage:
The things common to the three persons in that eternity were those internal acti ons of God, wherein the three persons did communicate: as 1. That one was in another, and possessed one another; the Father remaining with the Son, the Son with the Father, and the Holy Ghost in, P ov. 8.22 John 1.1 John 14.10 and with them both. Thus we read of Christ, the Lord possessed me, in the beginning of his way, before his works of old. And in the beginning was the word, and the word was with God. And I am in the Father, and the Father in me. 2. That one glorified another, John 17 5. the Father glorified the Son, and the Son glorified the Father, and the holy Ghost glorified both the Father and the Son: And now, O Father, glorifie thou me with thine own self, with the glory which I had with thee before the world was.

How does Spurgeon describe the initial spiritual fervor of believers in Sermon 2724?

Spurgeon teaches that the first outpouring of the Holy Spirit on a convert is likened to the fresh, refreshing moisture that covers the earth each morning. He writes, "Everything terrestrial has its dew in the morning, but its burning heat at noon," and adds, "When we were first converted, what a sparkling dew there was upon our leaf!" In this imagery, the early zeal of the believer is the "dew of the morning" that later may diminish as the heat of experience rises.

meta.heading: [Sermon 2724 — "The Dew of Christ's Youth"]
meta.passage:
Everything terrestrial has its dew in the morning, but its burning heat at noon, and we too, Beloved--I mean those of us who have received the anointing of the Holy Spirit--is not this too much the case even with us? When we were first converted, what a sparkling dew there was upon our leaf! We could not sing God's praises loudly enough! We could not sufficiently leap for joy before the Ark of the Lord. All the exultations of those who came before seemed utterly insufficient for us. There was, to us, such unction and savor in the Word of God that we could feast upon it everyday--yes, and all night long--and yet never be weary! We ran in the way of God's Commandments without weariness and we mounted aloft as on the wings of eagles and never thought that we could ascend too high. But, alas, Beloved, is it not the case with many of us that much of that early freshness of the morning of our youth is scattered, and some, at least, of our excellence has proved to be like the early cloud and the morning dew? Though in some things we trust that we have grown, yet we are compelled to confess that in some other things we have diminished. While in the depths of self-knowledge we feel that we have made progress, yet in the heights of joy in Christ, in the sublimities of a full devotion to Him, we sometimes fear that we have gone backward and that we have not the bliss of our youth, the dew of the morning.

Our text, speaking of our Lord Jesus Christ, says He has the dew of His youth.

According to Rutherford, what is the king’s role in relation to the church?

Rutherford asserts that the monarch is not merely a civil ruler but a divine appointment, stating that "the king, by office, is the church's nurse father" and describing him as "a sacred ordinance, the deputed power of God." This indicates that the king functions as a spiritual guardian and protector of the people, ordained to uphold divine law alongside the church’s authority.

According to Whitaker, how did Luther describe the Epistle of James in his 1525 preface?

Whitaker records that Luther, in his most ancient preface published at Wittenberg in 1525, “called it a strawen Epistle in comparison of the Epistles of Saint Peter and Saint Paul,” thereby expressing serious doubt about the authorship and argument of the Epistle of James, while Whitaker insists that Luther did not label the letter as “contentious, barren, swelling, or a strawen Epistle.”

Watson teaches that the spiritual mourner possesses a seed of comfort, describing it with the metaphor that “Light is sown for the righteous'” and affirming that “The mourner is heir to comfort”. What does Spurgeon say about the effect of biblical ignorance on a Christian’s peace in Sermon 3077?

Spurgeon teaches that a lack of scriptural knowledge brings sorrow and unsettles the heart, while greater understanding brings divine peace and happiness. He warns that "I would not have you to be ignorant, brethren," indicating that ignorance is an ill condition that should be shunned. He further explains that the more a Christian knows of his religion, "the better for his peace and for his happiness!" Thus, Spurgeon links deeper knowledge of the Gospel with the blessing of the Lord that "makes rich, and He adds no sorrow with it."

meta.heading: [Sermon 3077 — "Death--a Sleep"]
meta.passage: He that is rich towards God knows that "the blessing of the Lord, it makes rich, and He adds no sorrow with it." And he that is made wise unto salvation, has received that wisdom which "gives life to them that have it." If we had more celestial wisdom, I believe we would have more of heavenly joy and less of carnal sorrow. Many a Doctrine of the Gospel becomes the means of sadness and misery to the heart simply because it is not understood. Ignorance of the Bible often troubles men's hearts and consciences--and prevents them from finding that peace of God which a little more knowledge of it would be sure to give them. And I am certain that ignorance or forgetfulness of many of the exceedingly great and precious promises of God and of the marvelous things He has engaged to do for His people, often causes our eyes to flow with tears and our hearts to be overwhelmed with suffering. The more a Christian knows of his religion, the better for his peace and for his happiness! The Apostle says, "I would not have you to be ignorant, brethren." He knew that was an ill condition and we may well shun it. Depend upon this--the more thoroughly you understand the Gospel, the more you will find that the Gospel blesses you and makes you happy! Each word that Eternal Wisdom speaks is pure.

What time does Downame recommend for the devotional exercise and what reasons does he give for this recommendation?

Downame advises that the most proper occasion for the religious duty is "the first houre of the morning (as I suppose) is fittest for it". He argues this because, in the morning, the mind is refreshed after rest, the spirit is renewed, and the faculties of the soul are stronger. He adds that the early hour allows one to borrow an hour from sleep without hindering other responsibilities, reduces worldly distractions, and serves as a good preparation for the day's prayers.

What comforting argument does the Lord give using ravens to address believers worried about their material needs?

Spurgeon teaches that the Lord offers a comforting argument by pointing to the ravens, saying, "Consider the ravens: for they neither sow nor reap, which neither have storehouse nor barn, and God feeds them." This illustration shows that even creatures that do not labor are provided for, encouraging believers to trust in God's providential care for their temporal circumstances.

meta.heading: [Sermon 672 — "The Ravens' Cry"]
meta.passage:
Do not I, who provide for the old raven, provide for his young ones, both while they abide in the nest and when they wander for lack of meat?"

Solomon sent the sluggard to the ant, and learned, himself, lessons from conies, greyhounds, and spiders! Let us be willing to be instructed by any of God's creatures and go to the ravens' nest tonight to learn as in a school. To the pure nothing is unclean, and to the wise nothing is trivial. Let the superstitious dread the raven as a bird of ill omen, and let the thoughtless see nothing but a winged thing in glossy black--we are willing to see more, and doubtless shall not be unrewarded if we are but teachable.

Noah's raven brought him back no olive branch, but ours may! And it may even come to pass that ravens may bring us meat tonight as of old they fed Elijah by Cherith's brook. Our blessed Lord once derived a very potent argument from ravens--an argument intended to comfort and cheer those of His servants who were oppressed with needless anxieties about their temporal circumstances. To such he said, "Consider the ravens: for they neither sow nor reap, which neither have storehouse nor barn, and God feeds them.

According to Gill, what aspect of Christ’s humiliation demonstrates His active obedience in the state of humiliation?

Gill explains that Christ’s humiliation is shown in His willing assumption of the servant’s role, which is the concrete expression of His active obedience throughout His life. He notes that the Son of God "though he were a Son, yet learned he obedience by the things which he suffered!" and that He was called "Thou art my Servant, O Israel, in whom I will be glorified." By voluntarily becoming the Servant of God, Christ fulfilled the purpose of His obedience even to death, thereby embodying the humility required for the active obedience of His state of humiliation.

What signs at Christ’s baptism does Sermon 3298 cite as proof that He is the Son of God?

Sermon 3298 explains that John the Baptist testifies to Jesus’ divine sonship by pointing to three unmistakable signs: the heavenly sign that John had been instructed to watch for, the visible descent of the Spirit “in appearance like a dove” that “abode upon Him,” and the audible proclamation from the Father, "This is My Beloved Son, in whom I am well-pleased." Together these manifestations reveal the intimate union of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit and confirm Jesus as the Son of God.

meta.heading: [Sermon 3298 — "Lessons From Christ's Baptism"]
meta.passage:
And John bears witness that He is the Son of God because the sign from Heaven for which he had been told to look for had been given. As Jesus comes up out of the water, the Spirit of God descends upon Him in a visible shape-- in appearance like a dove--and rests upon Him. John says that "it abode upon Him," as though the Spirit was thenceforth to be His continual Companion and, truly, it was so. At the same time that the dove descended and lighted upon Christ, there was heard a Voice from Heaven, saying, "This is My Beloved Son, in whom I am well-pleased." This was the voice of God the Father--He did not reveal Himself in a bodily shape, but uttered wondrous words such as mortal ears had never before heard! The Father revealed Himself not to the eyes as the Spirit did, but to the ears--and the words He spoke clearly indicated that it was God the Father bearing witness to His beloved Son. So that the entrance of Christ upon His public ministry on earth was the chosen opportunity for the public manifestation of the intimate union between God the Father, God the Son and God the Holy Spirit!

Now, Sinner, from this day forward, if you have never done so before, think humbly, reverently and lovingly of all the three Persons of the most blessed Trinity in Unity! Bless the Son of God for becoming Man in order that He might redeem us from destruction. He left His Glory in Heaven and was made in the likeness of men that He might suffer in our place as the Lamb of God's Passover and that we might shelter beneath His sprinkled blood--and so escape the sword of vengeance.

According to Spurgeon’s sermon, what is David’s attitude toward Goliath’s blasphemies and how does he propose the enemy be dealt with?

Spurgeon teaches that David is consumed with righteous anger toward Goliath’s blasphemy, refusing to tolerate any insult against the Divine. He declares, "An insult against God cannot be allowed!" and insists that the blasphemer must be silenced. While David does not seek personal glory—"he is not so covetous of glory as to deprive a more deserving person of these huge materials for renown"—he urges that some hand must put Goliath down, just as he did with the lion: "When he kept his sheep and the lion came, David did not raise the question whether he could kill the lion--he killed him--and the question was settled." Thus, David’s response is one of decisive, unhesitant action to protect God’s name and people.

meta.heading: [Sermon 1810 — "The Lion and the Bear--Trophies Hung Up"]
meta.passage:
When David finds himself in the camp and when he hears Goliath of Gath pouring forth his blasphemies against Jehovah and defying Jehovah's people, David has no thought of having been mistaken in his former lofty adoration. He entertains no notion of adopting a lower style, but he inwardly burns with indignation against the infamous reviler. An insult against God cannot be allowed! This abominable blasphemer must be silenced. Somebody must put him down and so dispose of him that none shall ever dare, again, to do the same. David enquires whether somebody or other is not going to batter the bronze champion. If any man in the camp will meet this huge man-mountain, David will not stand in his way--he is not so covetous of glory as to deprive a more deserving person of these huge materials for renown. But it is imperative that some hand should silence that hillock of proud flesh! It is driven in upon David's devout heart that this blasphemous mouth must be shut and God's name and God's people must be clear of such a brutal enemy.

About the stilling of this enemy and avenger David has no enquiry to make. It is going to be done, done soon, and done without any particular display. When he kept his sheep and the lion came, David did not raise the question whether he could kill the lion--he killed him--and the question was settled.

What does Manton say about the difference between a second‑hand report and a personal witness of God's comfort?

Manton teaches that a second‑hand account lacks warmth, observing that "Report of a report is a cold thing, not valued, but a report of what we witness and experience ourselves comes warmly upon our hearts." He contrasts this genuine sharing of comfort with the empty chatter of carnal meetings, which he describes as filled with "stories of hawking and hunting, the best wine and delicious meats" and other worldly vanities that distract from the "high and excellent and necessary things of the grace of God in Christ." By emphasizing personal testimony, Manton urges believers to comfort others with the very comforts they have received from God.

What does Spurgeon say in Sermon 2549 about how a believer’s condition toward sin changes after conversion?

Spurgeon teaches that the believer, by union with Christ, passes from being enslaved by sin to being dead to it. He explains that just as "Christ being raised from the dead dies no more; death has no more dominion over Him," the Christian likewise experiences a reversal of power: "He is dead to sin and he ceases from it." The former lover of sin now hates it, and the Spirit’s work puts the sinner’s former master under his own foot. In this new state the believer has no desire to commit sin.

meta.heading: [Sermon 2549 — "Luminous Words"]
meta.passage:
"Christ being raised from the dead dies no more; death has no more dominion over Him. For in that He died, He died unto sin once: but in that He lives, He lives unto God. Likewise reckon you, also, yourselves, to be dead, indeed, unto sin, but alive unto God through Jesus Christ our Lord."

Now read between the lines of our text. In Christ we have died unto sin once, but now that we live unto God, we are as if we had actually died to sin and had passed into a new state and condition by virtue of our union with Jesus Christ our Lord. But while this is true, there is an experience of it which we have to undergo within our own spirits--hence the Apostle says, "Therefore since Christ has suffered for us in the flesh, arm yourselves, likewise, with the same mind." As He has died to sin, we are to die to sin, also. This takes place--the commencement of it, at any rate--at the time of conversion. The man who formerly loved sin begins to hate it. The sin which he used to swallow greedily, he now loathes and shuns. There is such a change worked by the Spirit of God in the heart of the Believer that sin can no more have dominion over him. It is dethroned from the place which it occupied over his nature. It once put its foot upon his neck, but now he puts his foot upon its neck. He is dead to sin and he ceases from it--not only that--in the sight of the all-seeing Jehovah, he has his infirmities, his failures and his sins, but still, as far as his heart is concerned, he has done with it.

There is not any sin which he would willingly do. There is no sin which he wishes to spare.

Why does the sermon say the Holy Spirit quotes the Old Testament in the New Testament?

Spurgeon teaches that the Holy Spirit quotes the Old Testament not to introduce new promises but to remind believers that the best expressions are those already given, saying that "He has said, I will never leave you, nor forsake you," and that "there are no better things in the world than the Words of God," and that by quoting the Pentateuch, Chronicles, and Isaiah the Spirit honors the Old Testament and shows that both Testaments are equally divine.

meta.heading: [Sermon 3150 — "Never, No Never, No Never"]
meta.passage:
You observe that the Apostle writes, "He has said, I will never leave you, nor forsake you," from which it plainly appears that Paul was quoting from Holy Writ. This should teach us how necessary it is for us, also, to quote Scripture whenever we can. The Holy Spirit abounds in gracious thoughts and in fitting language in which to express those thoughts, so He has no need to make extracts from what He has previously said. Yet He pleases to do so. Instead of giving us a new promise, He here gives us an old one over again, as if to remind us that there are no better things in the world than the Words of God, Himself, and that the very noblest expressions are those which have been already used!

Besides, the Holy Spirit here puts honor upon the Old Testament by quoting from it for the consolation of New Testament Believers. There are some persons who seem to think more of the New Testament than they do of the Old Testament. I have met with Christians in Germany with whom it has been quite a superstition that the Evangelists were superior to the Apostles and that the Apostles were superior to the Prophets. I trust that such notions as those will never spread among us! We see here that when an Apostle writes as an Inspired man, he quotes from the Pentateuch, he quotes from the Chronicles and he quotes from the prophecy of Isaiah--so that we are to honor the Old Testament and not to look upon it as a secondary book compared with the New Testament, but to reverence the Divine teaching in both portions of the Inspired Word.

According to Shedd in the Dogmatic Theology, what is the primary aim of retributive justice?

Shedd teaches that retributive justice is fundamentally retrospective, emphasizing that its purpose is not prospective reform but the repayment of past wrongdoing. He states that “Retributive justice is retrospective in its primary aim.” It “looks back at what has been done in the past” and its first object is “requital,” rather than moral improvement, deterrence, or future prevention.

What does Owen say about the mindset of fortunate Englishmen and their treatment of those who differ from them?

Owen observes that the spirit of men whose "fortune and power" tempt them to an insolency leads them to regard themselves as the sole true Englishmen and to desire that those who differ be "exterminated from their native soil." He concludes that such resolutions show little consistency with Christianity, humanity, or prudence.

How does Manton describe the way spiritual desires are developed compared to worldly desires?

Manton explains that worldly desires arise spontaneously, likening them to a nettle, whereas spiritual desires require intentional effort and cultivation. He writes, "Worldly desires, like a nettle, breed of their own accord, but spiritual desires need a great deal of cultivating." By encouraging believers to improve their tastes through experiencing the grace of God, Manton shows that tasting spiritual blessings awakens a lasting appetite, unlike the fleeting satisfaction of worldly cravings. He further warns that "If we are taken with other things, Christ loseth his sweetness and relish," indicating that neglecting spiritual desire dulls its fervor.

Why does Spurgeon say that a sinner should not look to other people for help?

Spurgeon teaches that a sinner’s only hope is divine, not human, assistance, because every honest person must acknowledge that "If the Lord does not help you, how can I help you?" He warns that humans are powerless to forgive sin or deliver souls from the dreadful fate of eternal fire, so the sinner must rely solely on God’s saving work.

meta.heading: [Sermon 3162 — "The Unfailing Help"]
meta.passage:
But "there is the dread of something after death"--that wrath to come of which the Word of God speaks in such solemn tones--that fire that never shall be quenched, that worm that dies not--it is that which haunts the sinner's conscience when he is once awakened to know his condition! And horrible as the story was in Samaria, it is not worse than the horrible fate that awaits every man who lives and dies unsaved!

Now it is no wonder at all, that when a man is awakened to see his great danger, standing as he does upon the edge of a precipice with a frightful gulf beneath him, he begins to appeal to anybody and everybody and to cry for help. So, tonight, I am going to begin by saying that in the case of the sinner, it is vain to look to man, for every honest man will have to say to such an one, "If the Lord does not help you, how can I help you?" You feel that you are in dreadful danger and you want to be saved--I beseech you, do not look to any of us, or to any of your fellow creatures for help, for we are quite powerless in the matter! God must save you! He must give you Christ or else you must die. We have no power to forgive your sins. There are some pretenders who surely ought to feel themselves out of place in this age, like owls in daylight, who still profess that they can pardon sin. It is a strange country, this. If a poor woman in a red cloak passes a farm and for sixpence tells a servant girl her fortune, she is put in prison.

What hope does the sermon “Stand Fast” describe for believers?

In Sermon 1688 — Spurgeon teaches that the believer’s hope is the “hope of full salvation”—the assurance that, because one has believed in Jesus Christ, one is presently free from all condemnation and will be forever free from condemnation for all sins. He adds that the One who removes the condemnation of sin will also destroy its power, enabling the believer “to love righteousness” and "to perfect holiness in the fear of the Lord." The sermon exhorts believers to “Be not moved away from the hope of the Gospel.”

meta.heading: [Sermon 1688 — "Stand Fast"]
meta.passage:
It is a series of skirmishes even when it does not assume the form of a pitched battle. He that would win Heaven must fight for it! He that would take the new Jerusalem must scale it and if he has the wits to take Jacob's ladder and set it against the wall and climb up that way, he will win the City. "The Kingdom of Heaven suffers violence and the violent take it by force."

At this time our subject is not the winning, but the wearing--not the taking but the holding of the fort. "Be not moved away," you that have come to it. "Be not moved away from the hope of the Gospel."

First, BE NOT MOVED AWAY FROM THE SUBJECT OF THAT HOPE so as to give up any part of the hope which is revealed to you by the Gospel. What is your hope? First, it is the hope of full salvation--the hope that, inasmuch as you have believed in Jesus Christ, you are free from all condemnation at the present moment and shall be free from all condemnation in the future as to all your sins. And that, in addition to this, He that takes away the condemnation of sin will also destroy the power of it over you. You have this hope--that being made to love righteousness you shall be enabled to walk in obedience and "to perfect holiness in the fear of the Lord."

Your hope is that one day you shall be presented holy, without blame and unreprovable in the sight of the great Father.

According to the sermon, how does the leafless tree image illustrate the state of Israel when its outward blessings are removed?

Spurgeon teaches that the leafless tree image shows that even when Israel appears barren and stripped of its visible blessings, its essential substance endures. He likens Israel to a terebinth or oak that may lose its foliage in harsh weather yet remains alive, stating that "the substance is in the tree when the leaves are gone." Thus, a faithful remnant persists despite apparent desolation.

meta.heading: [Sermon 121 — "The Leafless Tree"]
meta.passage:
"But," says God, "although this tenth only shall be preserved, and then even this small part shall be subjected to many perils yet Israel shall not be destroyed, for it shall be as a terebinth tree and as an oak;" their "substance is in them, when they cast their leaves," and so lose their verdure and their beauty; thus, in like manner, a holy seed, a chosen remnant, shall still be the substance of the children of Israel, when the fruitful land is stripped of its foliage, and that fair garden of earth is barren as the desert.

The figure is taken, first of all, from the terebinth or turpentine tree—here translated the teil tree. That tree is an evergreen, with this exception, that in very severe and inclement weather it loses its leaves; but even then the terebinth tree is not dead. And so of the oak; it loses its leaves every year, of course, but even then it is not dead. "So," says God, "you have seen the tree in winter, standing naked and bare, without any sign of life, its roots buried in the hard and frozen soil, and its naked branches exposed to every blast, without a bloom or a bud; yet the substance is in the tree when the leaves are gone.

What does Flavel say about how the law relates to the promise in the covenant?

Flavel argues that the law was not the ultimate end but was appended to the promise in order to serve the covenant’s purpose. He maintains that the gospel has priority over the law, yet the law retains useful functions as an appendix. In his discussion he writes, "the principality of the promise of life by Christ above the law", indicating that the promise of life in Christ stands supreme while the law remains a subordinate, consistent element.

What does Peter proclaim about salvation in Spurgeon's sermon titled "Grace--the One Way of Salvation"?

Spurgeon explains that Peter affirms the universal reach of salvation by stating, "We believe that through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ we shall be saved, even as they." This declaration is presented as an apostolic confession of faith, showing that salvation is by grace alone for both Jews and Gentiles.

meta.heading: [Sermon 765 — "Grace--the One Way of Salvation"]
meta.passage:
And then he concluded his address by saying, in effect, "Although these people are not circumcised, and ought not to be, yet we believe that there is no difference between the Jew and the Gentile, and by the Grace of our Lord Jesus Christ we shall be saved, even as they." Here Peter was not to be blamed, but to be greatly commended, for he spoke under the influence of the Spirit of God.

We shall use the text as concisely as we can for three important purposes. In the first place we shall look upon it AS AN APOSTOLIC CONFESSION OF FAITH. You notice it begins with, "We believe." We will call it, then, the "Apostle's Creed" and we may rest assured that it has quite as clear a right to that title as that highly esteemed composition which is commonly called the "Nicene, or Apostle's Creed."

Peter is speaking for the rest, and he says, "We believe." Well, Peter, what do you believe? We are all attentive. Peter's answer is, "We believe that through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ we shall be saved, even as they." There is a great deal of talk in our day--foolish, vainglorious, idiotic, senseless talk, as we think, about Apostolic succession. Some persons think they have the direct line from the Apostles running right at their feet, and others believe that those who make the greatest boast about it have the least claim to it.

What does Spurgeon say about the number and nature of the advents each person experiences in his sermon "Two Advents Of Christ"?

Spurgeon teaches that every individual will experience two distinct advents. He writes, "Every man will have two advents--the advent which he now enjoys or which he now misuses upon earth--and the advent which lies beyond the present course of probation." The first advent is the present earthly life, in which a person lives and either enjoys or misuses his time. The second advent occurs after death, when the soul returns to a resurrected body to stand before judgment and receive its appointed doom. Spurgeon parallels this with Christ’s own two advents: His first coming in death and His second coming as Judge.

meta.heading: [Sermon 430 — "Two Advents Of Christ"]
meta.passage:
"By one man sin entered into the world and death by sin." That is the first fact. "But now once in the end of the world has He appeared to put away sin by the sacrifice of Himself." This is the second fact.

But you have not got the full weight of the comparison yet. After man's spirit has been once on earth, has lived its time, and the body has died, the soul is to revisit this earth again, for "after this the judgment." Every man will have two advents--the advent which he now enjoys or which he now misuses upon earth--and the advent which lies beyond the present course of probation. After he has descended to the tomb, he shall come here again. His bones shall come together, bone to his bone. The flesh shall come upon the skeleton and the spirit shall return, either from the Heaven where it rejoices, or from the Hell where it howls, to inhabit the body once again, and to stand upon the earth.

We must all come here again--even though the place that now knows us shall know us no more forever. Yet, somewhere upon this earth we shall stand, even though we should be unable to recognize any likeness between that and the place in which we lived, and unable to recognize any likeness between us and what we were. Regardless, here we must return to receive our appointed doom.

Now, so is it with Christ. He has once died and He is to come a second time. A second time is His body to be on earth. After death, the judgment! Only when we speak of Christ, He shall come, not to be judged but to be the Judge. After death comes the reward with us--after death the reward with Him.

According to Calvin in Tracts Vol 3, what role does charity play in the righteousness that justifies a believer?

Calvin teaches that true faith, prompted by repentance, brings the believer into the promise of the Holy Spirit and produces charity, which together with hope form the complete righteousness by which one is justified. What does Spurgeon teach about the necessity of personal prayer compared to liturgical or extemporaneous prayer?

Spurgeon teaches that each believer must bring his own personal supplication before God, because "What is your petition, and it shall be granted you. And what is your request...it shall be performed." He warns that "any form of prayer--liturgical or extempore--can meet the needs of your case at all times." Instead, he urges believers to offer private petitions, likening the power of silent, personal prayer to Hannah’s silent lips and the comfort of a sorrowful spirit in secret fellowship with God. This emphasis on individualized prayer is presented as suitable for newcomers to the divine life as well as for the venerable and wise.

meta.heading: [Sermon 2487 — "Ordered Steps"]
meta.passage:
I hoped, just now, when we were praying, that my words might suit the cases of many of you, but I felt more concerned that each one should be offering petitions and the thanksgivings for himself. Oh, what power there often is in those personal prayers where there is no audible voice, but only the lips move, as did Hannah's! At such times the woman of a sorrowful spirit goes her way comforted because of her secret fellowship with God. Do not imagine that any form of prayer--liturgical or extempore--can meet the needs of your case at all times. No, you must present your own personal supplication, and the Lord seems to say to you, as Ahasuerus said to Esther, "What is your petition, and it shall be granted you. And what is your request...it shall be performed."

It seems to me that my text may suit all of us who are in this assembly. I am sure that it suits me. I have prayed it before I have preached from it and I desire to be praying it while I am preaching concerning it. I commend it to those who are just beginning the Divine Life and I suggest it as equally appropriate to those who may have wandered somewhat out of the way of holiness. Yes, and I suggest it to those who are venerable and full of wisdom.

According to Sermon 1179, what attitude should a believer adopt as they enter the later years of life?

Spurgeon teaches that as a believer enters the later years, a cheerful heart should be kept while also becoming more solemnly earnest, with a grave consideration of eternal things. He emphasizes that "'Tis time to live if I grow old." and that "Wisdom dictates, in old age, if never before, that a grave consideration of eternal earth should be more under foot and Heaven should be more in the heart." Moreover, he warns that works among fellow men will soon be impossible, urging believers to redeem the time while they still can. Thus the sermon calls for a balance of cheerfulness, earnestness, and focus on heavenly matters in old age.

meta.heading: [Sermon 1179 — "Forty Years"]
meta.passage:
At the same time, ripe years are not to be trifled with. We have known some who have treated the fact that they are advancing in life with unbecoming levity--their gray hairs show that they are nearing the bounds of life, but they are as thoughtless as if they were yet in their minority--and so they are an incongruous miniature of the weakness of age and the frivolity of youth. It is well to keep a cheerful heart to the last hour--and no man has so much reason for doing so as a believer in Jesus! But, at the same time, it is surely time to be solemnly earnest when one has passed the prime of life. Wisdom dictates, in old age, if never before, that a grave consideration of eternal earth should be more under foot and Heaven should be more in the heart.

Every year should increase our sense of the certainty, value and nearness of eternal things. "'Tis time to live if I grow old." Works for God among our fellow men will soon be impossible to us--let us be diligent in them while as yet our sun is above the horizon. Now, if ever, we should redeem the time, because the days are evil. In the very middle of life, when strength is in our bones and we have the most grand possibilities of vigorous service, it is well for us to be fully alive to the highest interests and purposes. We should not be spending a dreamy existence, as if we were mere lotus eaters, born into a garden of poppies to sleep all day.

According to Owen, what was the primary purpose of the spiritual gift of wisdom in the early church and how did it affect those who opposed the gospel?

Owen teaches that the spiritual gift of wisdom was essentially a defensive ability, stating that "this gift of wisdom, in the first place, was a spiritual skill" for defending the truths of the gospel when they were questioned, opposed, or blasphemed. He describes how, in primitive times, unlearned believers were able to "maintain and defend the truth" before doctors, scribes, lawyers, rulers of synagogues, princes and kings, thereby "confounding their adversaries" and driving obstinate unbelievers "to cover their shame by betaking themselves unto rage and bestial fury." While Owen affirms this special function, he also notes that the wisdom is not absolutely confined to that use alone.

What does Dabney argue is the flaw in the Pelagian claim that the power of example alone accounts for the universal tendency toward sin?

Dabney points out that the Pelagian reliance on a merely evil example fails because, as he notes, "If there were no innate tendency to evil, a bad example would usually repel and disgust the holy soul." He argues that the uniform and certain result of sin across humanity shows that an innate tendency to evil must be operative, not just external examples, and that attributing the result to God's natural law would make God appear the author of sin more than the Calvinistic explanation does.

According to Spurgeon in Sermon 660, how does the Holy Spirit bring spiritual light to humanity?

Spurgeon teaches that humanity is "dark, dark, dark" and dwells in the black darkness of sin until the Holy Spirit renews it, granting the "true Light which lights every man which comes into the world." He points out that no one has even a spark of spiritual light unless it is received from above, and that the Spirit’s work begins mysteriously in the heart. Spurgeon illustrates this mystery with the image: "The wind blows where it wishes and you hear the sound of it, but cannot tell from where it comes and where it goes: so is everyone that is born of the Spirit." He also recalls the first divine act of creation, "The Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters," as a prefigure of the Spirit’s renewing power. In this way, the Holy Spirit silently and efficaciously quickens the dead heart, excites emotions, longings, and desires, bringing spiritual illumination to those chosen.

meta.heading: [Sermon 660 — "Light--Natural And Spiritual"]
meta.passage:
They are still darkness, naturally, until God the Holy Spirit comes to renew them.

In the whole world, whether it is among kings, statesmen, or Divines, there is not one who has so much as a spark of spiritual light unless he has received it from above. And he can only have received it from above through Him who is "the true Light which lights every man which comes into the world," who is enlightened at all. Dark, dark, dark is the whole of humanity--it dwells in the black darkness of sin and must perish there unless the same Divine power which said, "Let there be light," of old, shall bestow spiritual light. You observe that the first Divine action in connection with the formation and shaping of the world, was this--"The Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters."

The secret work of the Holy Spirit begins in the human heart--we cannot always say precisely when or how. "The wind blows where it wishes and you hear the sound of it, but cannot tell from where it comes and where it goes: so is everyone that is born of the Spirit." In the hearts of God's chosen ones this Spirit works mysteriously and silently, but most efficaciously. The expression translated, "moved upon," conveys in the original the idea of a bird brooding over its nest. The Holy Spirit mysteriously quickens the dead heart, excites emotions, longings, desires.

It may be some of you are feeling His operations this morning. You have not yet received the Divine light, but there are workings of the Divine energy in your spirit.

According to Watson, what is the essential condition for performing duties in a spiritual manner?

Watson teaches that the decisive factor is the condition of the heart rather than the amount of outward activity. He stresses that believers must keep their souls pure, avoiding any “tincture of uncleanness,” because a heart steeped in sin cannot “burn in holy devotion.” He explains that true spiritual service is marked by quality, noting "'tis not how much we do, but how well" and that "the heart makes the Non chordula musica sed cor." In other words, a heart alive to God’s Spirit gives life to duty, while a dead or sinful heart renders worship ineffective.

What does Systematic Theology Vol2 teach about the role of merit in the doctrine of salvation?

Systematic Theology Vol2 asserts that introducing merit into the plan of redemption corrupts its very nature, stating that salvation is entirely a work of grace. It declares that "the salvation of sinful men is a matter of grace" and emphasizes that God sent His Son and Holy Spirit to apply that grace, without any human contribution. Consequently, all goodness in humanity is attributed to the Holy Spirit, and spiritual blessings are seen as the fruits of election, not personal merit.

What reason does Perkins give in the Golden Chain for claiming that death is more excellent than life?

Perkins teaches that death is superior to life because it secures the soul’s entrance into the presence of the King of kings and guarantees eternal fellowship with God, while the body remains subject to decay. He states that “death is more excellent then life” and describes the body as lying in “darke and loathsome graues, and there be wasted and consumed by wormes,” yet the soul enjoys everlasting communion with the Father, Christ, and the Holy Ghost. This contrast between the corruptible flesh and the incorruptible heavenly fellowship forms the basis of his claim.

How does Sermon 1549 explain the relationship between divine sovereignty and the promise to give freely to those who are thirsty?

Sermon 1549 explains that divine sovereignty does not limit the generosity of the Gospel, but rather works hand‑in‑hand with it. The sermon states that although “He will have mercy on whom He will have mercy and He will have compassion on whom He will have compassion,” the sovereign will still fulfill the invitation to give, declaring “I will give unto him that is thirsty of the fountain of the water of life freely.” Thus, the doctrine of election and sovereign grace is presented as compatible with an open, generous invitation to all who come to Christ.

meta.heading: [Sermon 1549 — "Good News For Thirsty Souls"]
meta.passage:
Thus He proved that He assuredly meant what He said and meant that it should stand good through all ages--"I will give unto him that is thirsty of the fountain of the water of life freely." It is to be noticed, too, that our Lord spoke these words as a King--"He that sat upon the Throne said, Behold, I make all things new," and then He added, "I will give unto him that is thirsty of the fountain of the water of life freely." Divine Sovereignty, therefore, is not opposed to the most generous promises of the Gospel! Jesus Christ may give or withhold as He pleases--but His will is to give.

He will have mercy on whom He will have mercy and He will have compassion on whom He will have compassion, but the stern truth of His infinite Sovereignty is coupled with the sweet declaration of boundless charity--"I will give unto him that is thirsty of the fountain of the water of life freely." However much we preach the Doctrines of Election and Divine Sovereignty, we never intend to limit the Grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, but as freely as if we had not believed in Sovereignty to publish our Lord's generous Gospel words, "Him that comes unto Me I will in no wise cast out." Again, the doctrine that salvation in us as well as for us is entirely the work of God, is not opposed to the most open invitation to come to Christ, for the verse out of which we have culled our text begins thus--"I am Alpha and Omega, the Beginning and the End," that is to say, "I am the Founder and Finisher of salvation.

Which early church fathers does Aa Hodge cite as supporting infant baptism as an apostolic tradition?

In Aa Hodge Outlines Of Theology, Hodge records that several early Christian writers affirm infant baptism as an apostolic tradition. He notes that Justin Martyr (a.d. 138) says, "There were among Christians of his time, many persons of both sexes, some sixty and some seventy years old, who had been made disciples of Christ from their infancy." Irenaeus (born about a.d. 97) declares that "He came to save all by himself; all I say who by him are born again unto God, infants, and little children and youths." Origen (a.d. 185) observes that it was "the usage of the church to baptize infants," and adds that "the church had received the tradition from the apostles." Cyprian (bishop of Carthage, a.d. 248‑258) and his synod mandated infant baptism before the eighth day, and Augustine (a.d. 358) affirms that this "doctrine is held by the whole church, not instituted by councils, but always retained." Thus Hodge presents a continuous patristic witness to infant baptism as apostolic.

What two conditions does Hodge say Roman Catholic theology requires for a sacrament to be efficacious?

Hodge explains that Roman Catholic teaching holds the efficacy of a sacrament on the part of the administrator to two essential conditions. First, the minister must be "canonically authorized"—for the sacraments of orders and confirmation he must be a bishop in communion with the pope, and for the other sacraments he must be a regular popish priest; the personal character of the bishop or priest, even if he be in mortal sin, does not prevent the effect. Second, the minister must exercise the positive intention to do what the church intends, because "To the valid performance of the sacrament is required the intention upon the part of the officiating minister of doing that which the church does."

According to Spurgeon in Sermon 3065, why is the third Beatitude considered a higher order than the first two?

Spurgeon teaches that the third Beatitude is superior because meekness is a positive virtue that extends outward toward others, rather than being merely an internal condition. He observes that "the meekness has to do with other people." Unlike the first two characteristics, which are wrapped up in the self—poverty in spirit and personal mourning—meekness is manifested in a man’s dealings with his fellow men, making it a larger, more expansive virtue that works in a wider sphere and grows out of the earlier Beatitudes.

meta.heading: [Sermon 3065 — "The Third Beatitude"]
meta.passage: Note too that this third Beatitude is of a higher order than the other two. There is something positive in it as to virtue. The first two are rather expressive of deficiency, but here there is a something supplied. A man is poor in spirit-- that is, he feels that he lacks a thousand things that he ought to possess. The man mourns--that is, he laments over his state of spiritual poverty. But now there is something really given to him by the Grace of God--not a negative quality, but a positive proof of the work of the Holy Spirit within his soul so that he has become meek. The first two characteristics that receive a benediction appear to be wrapped up in themselves. The man is poor in spirit--that relates to himself. His mourning is his own personal mourning which ends when he is comforted. But the meekness has to do with other people. It is true that it has a relationship to God, but a man's meekness is especially towards his fellow men. He is not simply meek within himself--his meekness is manifest in his dealings with others. You would not speak of a hermit who never saw a fellow creature as being meek. The only way in which you could prove whether he was meek would be to put him with those who would try his temper. So that this meekness is a virtue--larger, more expansive, working in a wider sphere than the first two characteristics which Christ has pronounced blessed. It is superior to the others, as it should be, since it grows out of them. Yet, at the same time, as there is through the whole of the Beatitudes a fall parallel with the rise, so is it here.

What does Spurgeon say is the purpose of God sealing a person's hand during sickness?

Spurgeon teaches that when God seals a man's hand in sickness He is providing a quiet season for reflection, so that the busy soul may turn its focus toward heavenly matters. He writes, "Thus is our hand sealed from its occupation that our heart may be unsealed towards God, Heaven and eternal things!" This sealing removes the ability to work on earthly tasks, inviting the afflicted to contemplate divine truths and seek the blessing that comes from such meditation.

meta.heading: [Sermon 3289 — "The Sealed Hand--a Winter Sermon"]
meta.passage:
In the sickbed for weeks and months, God seals up the active hand, and thus He presents to the busy a quiet season for reflection! In France, they call the hospital, "the House of God," and it is well when it becomes so. The man who will not think of God if he can help it, while he is busy in the world, is, by sickness blessed with time for consideration and, being set aside from turmoil, he is invited to rise above his engrossing cares! The Great Father seems to say, "Lie there alone. Lie awake through the night-watches and think of your past ways and what they lead to. Listen to the tick of the clock and mark the flight of time till you number your days and apply your heart unto wisdom. Your own work you cannot touch. Now, therefore, think of the work of your God and Savior till you obtain the blessing which comes of it." This is the design of sickness and inability to follow our calling! Thus is our hand sealed from its occupation that our heart may be unsealed towards God, Heaven and eternal things!--

It is clear that God can easily seal up the hand of man if he uses his strength in rebellion or folly, for He has other seals besides sickness. When the wicked are determined to carry out a plan which is not according to His mind, He can baffle them. See the people gathering on the plain of Shinar, bringing together brick and slime that they may build a tower whose lofty height shall mark the center of a universal monarchy! What does God do?

What analogies does the sermon use to illustrate people’s refusal to accept Christ’s salvation?

The sermon illustrates the refusal by comparing it to situations where no one objects to a benefactor: "Men in a dungeon do not take exception to the man who breaks open their prison and sets them free!" It also mentions that dying men do not generally object to the physician who seeks to save their lives, and a condemned man does not quarrel with a king who gives him a free pardon. By citing these images, the preacher argues that the greatest evidence of sin’s “strange infatuation” is that a person "quarrels with his best Friend" and rejects the plan of salvation.

meta.heading: [Sermon 3258 — "Stumbling at the Word"]
meta.passage:
They prefer to be lost rather than to be saved by such a Savior in such a way as He has ordained!

Men in a dungeon do not take exception to the man who breaks open their prison and sets them free! Men who are dying do not generally object to the physician who is seeking to save their lives. A man who is condemned to death does not quarrel with the king who gives him a free pardon! There is nothing which shows the strange infatuation of sin more than this--that a man quarrels with his best Friend, puts away from him the plan of salvation which God has made with Infinite Wisdom and will not come to Christ that he may have life! I want, as the Holy Spirit shall help me, to plead with all those in this assembly to whom Christ, Himself, has hitherto been "a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense"-- those who still "stumble at the Word, being disobedient."

I shall try, first, to plead with you against your objections. Then I will endeavor to plead with you for Christ And after that I willplead with God'speople for you and ask them to plead with God on your behalf

First, then, let me PLEAD WITH YOU AGAINST YOUR OBJECTIONS.

What is it that makes you think so little of Christ, or that makes you think so badly of Christ? Shall I take the words out of your mouth? It may be that one reason of your quarrel is that Christ's commands seem to you to be so strict He will have you pluck out your right eye and cut off your right arm if they would prevent you from entering into life.

How does the sermon describe the relationship between the Holy Spirit’s power and the Gospel in the present age compared to the apostolic era?

Spurgeon teaches that the Holy Spirit’s power behind the Gospel is unchanged from the apostolic age to the present. He affirms that "the power which rendered the Gospel saving in the olden times was not Paul's logic, or Apollo's eloquence--the saving power lay in the Holy Spirit accompanying the Divine Truth." Moreover, he declares that "He is just as able to make the Word of God the power of God unto salvation, today, as He was then!" Thus, the same divine empowerment that saved in the first century continues to work today, whether in far‑off lands like Madagascar or in the preacher’s own midst.

meta.heading: [Sermon 3518 — "The Powerful Truth of God"]
meta.passage: More than that, we have the same spirit resting upon the Gospel, now, as then! The power which rendered the Gospel saving in the olden times was not Paul's logic, or Apollo's eloquence--the saving power lay in the Holy Spirit accompanying the Divine Truth. Now the Spirit of God is not straitened. He is Divine. His arm is not shortened that He cannot save. He is just as able to make the Word of God the power of God unto salvation, today, as He was then! Yes, and I bless His name, He is doing it! He has been doing it lately in Madagascar, as an instance in far-off lands, and we have seen Him do it in our very midst. We have known and conversed with multitudes who have been turned from darkness to light, from the slavery of Satan into the liberty of Christ by the power of the Gospel which Paul preached, which we, also, preach! When Paul and his two or three companions came into Ephesus, they were not one whit different from two or three Christians going into any city in the world with the view of evangelizing it! Of course, they had the gift of miracles, but we have other appliances which they had not. We have books which we can scatter far and wide--and we have an amount of religious liberty in almost every place which they did not possess.

According to Spurgeon in this sermon, what specific title does he encourage believers to use for Christ to express a deeper love?

Spurgeon teaches that believers should move beyond the title of trust and address Christ with a heartfelt declaration of love, urging them to call Him "O You whom my soul loves." He emphasizes that this expression reflects the pure, Spirit‑born flame of love that should replace mere simple faith.

What does Calvin say about the relationship between keeping God's commandments and the basis of our confidence in prayer?

Calvin teaches that keeping God's commandments does not make confidence in prayer dependent on human works, but rather shows that true religion and sincere worship are inseparable from faith. He explains, "because we keep his commandments, he means not that confidence in prayer is founded on our works;" and illustrates the point with the analogy, "Because the sun shines over us at midday, there is more heat;" indicating that a causal expression does not always denote a causal origin.

meta.heading: [Calvin — Commentary Catholic Epistles]
meta.passage:
By saying, because we keep his commandments, he means not that
 confidence in prayer is founded on our works; but he teaches this only,
 that true religion and the sincere worship of God cannot be separated
 from faith. Nor ought it to appear strange that he uses a causal
 particle, though he does not speak of a cause; for an inseparable
 addition is sometimes mentioned as a cause as when one says, Because
 the sun shines over us at midday, there is more heat; but it does not
 follow that heat comes from light.

What does Sedgwick identify as the cause of despair in a secret sinner?

Sedgwick teaches that despair arises when the sinner perceives divine justice as overwhelming and a cloud over the mercy‑seat, causing the soul to sink. He writes, "when the soul sees justice to be exceeding great, and a cloud over the mercy-seat, now it sinks a pace," and explains that this perception of great sin makes divine justice seem terrible, leading to hopelessness.

What does Calvin define as the perfect love of God in his commentary on 1 John 2:7‑11?

Calvin teaches that the perfect love of God is defined as "the complete keeping of his law". He explains that this love is the standard for believers, urging each person to aspire to this perfection according to the measure of grace given to him. Moreover, Calvin asserts that true progress in faith occurs only when one "cleaves from the heart to God," indicating that genuine communion with the Father and the Son is demonstrated through love and obedience.

What does Sermon 884 say about the pursuit of happiness through sin?

Spurgeon teaches that chasing happiness by sinful means only drives it farther away. He writes, "The more intensely you pursue happiness in the bewitching way of sin, the further will it fly from you." The sermon warns that such pursuit leads to danger, weariness, and a shipwreck of the soul, and that true peace is found only in a covenant with God.

meta.heading: [Sermon 884 — "Help for Seekers of the Light"]
meta.passage:
The more intensely you pursue happiness in the bewitching way of sin, the further will it fly from you. Like the will-'o-the-wisp, the glare of pleasure will entice you into the quagmire and there will leave you to find that your chase has gained you nothing but danger and weariness. The pearl of happiness lies not in the depths of dissipation. The broad road always ends in destruction, never in peace.

Hoist the sails of desire to the breeze, let go the helm of reason and let your soul be borne wherever the blasts of temptation or the currents of custom may direct and one thing you may be sure of--your unhappy boat will never be drifted by such means into the haven of peace! To such a voyage shipwreck is the certain end! To other modes of living disappointment is in like manner attached. Vain is it to pile up gold. Vain is it to awaken the clarion trumpet of fame. Vain is it to gather learning or to master eloquence, eminence, rank, wealth, power--all these things are too little to satisfy the insatiable craving of an immortal soul.

You must have God or you shall never have enough! You must be reconciled to Him or you can never be at peace with yourself. Man must enter into a covenant of peace with his God or all the creatures of God shall conspire against him! Pilgrim of earth, your way must be towards holiness and God, or in vain shall you expect the dawning--to the sinner there is reserved the blackness of darkness forever and even now his way is hard and his path is darkened with fear and disquietude.

Who does Owen identify as the legitimate governors that could determine the liberty of Jewish Christians, and how does he distinguish them from false apostles?

Owen argues that the only legitimate governors who could make such a determination were the apostles themselves, noting that the decision was “a doctrinal declaration of the mind of the Holy Ghost” rather than an act of church power. He contrasts these lawful governors with the “false apostles” who “were none of their lawful governors, but went about as seducers, drawing away the disciples of the apostles from them.”

(1.) The governors of the Christian church which made the deter-

What does Owen claim about the king’s role in granting indulgences and its relation to the peace of the kingdom?

Owen argues that the monarch is uniquely qualified to decide whether an indulgence serves the nation’s stability, stating that the king is "the best and most competent judge of what will contribute to the peace of the kingdom" and that his royal intentions are guided by a clear understanding of their consistency with the kingdom’s welfare. He further expresses confidence that the king’s declarations have not been undermined and that a peaceful conduct by the subjects will aid the king’s successful governance.

What does Burroughs identify as the primary cause that leads the poor and discontented to become witches?

Burroughs teaches that the root of witchcraft is personal discontent. He explains that the Devil and targets those whose spirits are "vexed" and "discontent at home," especially the poor, old, and melancholy. According to Burroughs, "the ground of all those that have been witches" is this inner dissatisfaction, which the Devil exploits by "fastens his temptations"—promising money to the poor or vengeance to the angry—thereby drawing them into unlawful courses.

Why does Reynolds say an aged man needs spectacles to read small print in the Treatise of the Passions?

Reynolds teaches that the aged man's difficulty in reading small print stems from a double defect: his bodily power is weakened and the letters lack sufficient materiality for his limited understanding. He illustrates this with the familiar similitude, stating that "an Aged man is not able to read a small Print, with out the Assistance of Spectacles to make the Letters by a refraction seeme greater." Thus the uncertainty of opinion arises from both the insufficiency of the understanding and the disproportion of the object to that understanding.

meta.heading: [Reynolds — Treatise Of The Passions]
meta.passage:
Even so also the Ob jects of mans Vnderstanding must participate of the two contr

 ries, Abstraction and Materi ality. Abstraction first, in proportion to the
 
 of the Vnderstanding, which is Spi rituall. And Materiality too, in respect of the Sense, on which the Vnderstanding de pends in this estate, as on the Medium of Conveyance, and that is Corporall. So that where ever there is Difficulty and Vncertain ty of Operation in the Vnderstanding, there is a double defect and disproportion: first in the Power, whose Operations are restrained and limited for the most, by the Body: and then in the Object, which hath not a suffici ent mixture of those two qualities, which should proportion it to the Power. This is plaine by a familiar similitude; an Aged man is not able to read a small Print, with out the Assistance of Spectacles to make the Letters by a refraction seeme greater. Where first wee may descry an Imperfection in the Organ; for if his Eyes were as cleare

and well-dispos'd as a young mans, hee would be able by his Naturall Power, without Art, to receive the Species of small Letters. And next, there is an Imperfection and deficiencie in the Letters; for if they had the same Mag nitude and fitnesse in themselves, which they seeme to have by Refraction through the Glasse, the weaknesse of his power might haply have sufficient strength to receive them without those Helps. So that alwayes the Uncertainty of Opinion is grounded on the In sufficiencie of the Vnderstanding to receive an Object, and on the Disproportion of the Object to the Nature of the Vnderstanding.

What does Binning say about the proper way believers should regard the redemption they receive through Christ?

Binning teaches that believers ought to regard redemption not merely as a duty or task but as a privilege and dignity granted by Christ. He urges that one should "look upon it as the one half, and greater half of the benefite conferred by Christs death" rather than seeing it only as a requirement, because this perspective encourages gratitude and a deeper sense of the sufficiency of Christ’s work. By viewing redemption as a gracious gift, the believer is led to groan for the full redemption of both soul and body, seeking complete freedom from the law of sin.
